stem: A 28-year-old man undergoes an HRCT after complaints of chronic cough and phlegm production. He is known to be a user of recreational drugs.
prompt: Which of the following findings is NOT likely to be found? Select ONE answer only.
options: Air space opacification in the lower lobes bilaterally
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which finding is NOT likely to be found.

Talcosis causes hypERdense nodules, not hypOdense nodules.

There are a number of ways in which recreational drug use can affect the patient and be seen radiologically.

Talcosis - embolisation of particulate matter injected intravenously gives rise to centrilobular micronodules which may be high density.

Septic emboli - secondary to non-sterile intravenous injection and endocardial vegetations. Cavitating lung nodules associated with clinical manifestations of infection.

Apical bullae/pneumothorax - associated with inhalational drugs, cannabis, cocaine, ecstasy, amphetamines

Pulmonary oedema - Perihilar airspace opacification with or without pleural effusions. Associated with cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine use.

Consolidation - straightforward lower respiratory tract infection secondary to atypical lifestyle, concurrent immunosuppression, or aspiration during periods of reduced consciousness.

Nasal septum destruction - associated with snorting cocaine, due to vasoconstriction and necrosis.

Skin abscesses and pseudoaneurysm - formation at injection sites

stem: A 68-year-old man with increasing dyspnoea and a history of asbestos exposure has a CT scan. The CT shows bilateral pleural thickening with calcification and a 3cm rounded lower lobe mass. There is pleural thickening with bronchovascular markings coursing from it towards the hilum in a curved path. Post-contrast there is enhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Round atelectasis

Round atelectasis occurs most commonly as part of the spectrum of asbestos related findings but does have other lesser aetiologies. It is also referred to as ‘infolded lung’ which better describes the appearances seen on CT. On CT there is a rounded mass-like region adjacent to the pleural surface. A comet tail sign is seen coming from the mass where the bronchovascular structures supplying the affected part of the lung are pulled into the centre of it thus there is a linear opacity curving outwards from the mass and pointing towards the hilum. The pleura adjacent to the mass is often thickened and if the mass is sufficiently large, features of volume loss can be seen in the ipsilateral hemithorax. Owing to the association with asbestos the patient may well show other features of exposure such as pleural plaque disease.

Malignant mesothelioma

This is an aggressive malignancy of the pleura which has an extremely strong association to prior asbestos exposure. It spreads around the pleura creating a rind over the lung in some cases, as well as spreading along the fissures and spreading to involve the mediastinum. Direct invasion of the chest wall occurs and is best investigated for with MRI. PET/CT also has a role to play in making the distinction from benign pleural thickening as well as establishing the nodal extent of the disease. Calcification, if it is seen in association with a diagnosis of malignant mesothelioma, is due to engulfment of pleural plaques as opposed to tumour calcium production.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma does occur far more commonly in patients with a history of asbestos exposure than malignant mesothelioma, however the latter is frequently paired with asbestos exposure in a question setting. This is because there are only a tiny number of malignant mesothelioma cases who do not have any appreciable asbestos exposure whereas squamous cell carcinoma also occurs readily in asbestos naive patients.

Although a third of squamous cell carcinomas of the lung are peripherally located it is mainly found as a central cavitating mass. When it does occur in the peripheral lung, chest wall invasion is an important feature to observe for.

Hamartoma

Fat within a thoracic mass is diagnostic of a hamartoma but is only seen in approximately half of cases. Hamartomas are very similar to the chondromas which form part of the Carney triad (pulmonary chondromas, gastric leiomyosarcomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas). NB this is different from Carney complex (atrial myxoma, facial/buccal pigmentation, sertoli tumours of the testis and multiple other findings).

Pleural fibroma

Pleural fibromas are benign fibrous tumours. Unlike their malignant counterpart, the malignant mesothelioma, pleural fibromas do not have an association with prior asbestos exposure. Pleural fibromas tend to be asymptomatic unless large and causing symptoms related to mass effect. There is however a reasonably strong association with hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy.

On CT the tumours are smooth with contrast enhancement. If seen on a CXR, the presence of an obtuse angle between the bulk of the mass and the chest wall strongly suggests a pleural mass (as opposed to a parenchymal one). Some fibromas can be pedunculated. The presence of haemorrhage or necrosis raises the suspicion of malignancy and although these tumours themselves are benign, around a third of them undergo malignant transformation. Surgical excision, therefore, is the usual management approach.

stem: A 45-year-old lady is being investigated for atypical chest pains which she has been experiencing for the last two months. She is worried as she has a strong family history of heart problems. She undergoes a 24-hour ECG which is normal, but an exercise ECG shows some lateral T-wave inversion. An adenosine stress MRI is planned for further evaluation.
prompt: Which of the following is a contra-indication to an Adenosine stress MRI? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Adenosine stress MRI has overtaken dobutamine stress MRI in terms of sensitivity and specificity for investigating the presence of ischaemia or infarction. Adenosine causes coronary vasodilation. If there is a haemodynamically significant stenosis to a coronary vessel, the vessels distal to the stenosis are already maximally dilated to maximise flow and thus the application of adenosine makes no difference to the vessel calibre or the resultant perfusion. Furthermore, the vasodilatation to the remaining unoccluded vessels can 'steal' blood from the stenosed territory and this is seen as hypoperfusion to the affected territory. Dipyridamole (antiplatelet), blocks uptake of adenosine and so patients taking this are also poor candidates for this test, however dipyridimole itself can also induce vasodilatation so may be used as an agent in its own right instead of adenosine.

Contraindications to adenosine include:

Second or third degree heart block

Bronchospasm

Hypotension <90mmHg systolic

Myocardial infarction within 48hrs

Uncontrolled arrhythmia

Severe/critical aortic stenosis

The half-life of adenosine is exceptionally short, around 10 seconds, thus any side effects experienced during the scan resolve very quickly. It also means that during the scan, in order to maintain the effect, the adenosine must be given as an infusion.

stem: Of the right paratracheal line, which of the following best describes its anatomical limitations?
prompt: Select one answer only:
options: The interface of the parietal and visceral pleura meeting anteromedially
The interface of the right lung and mediastinal reflection of the azygos vein.
The interface of the right lung and posterior mediastinal soft tissue
The opposition of the pleural surfaces of the posteromedial surfaces of the upper lobes posteriorly to the oesophagus
The right tracheal wall adjacent to the pleural surface
explanation:
The azygo-oesophageal recess is formed by the interface of the right lung and the mediastinal reflection of the azygos vein.

The anterior junctional line is formed by the meeting of the parietal and visceral pleura anteromedially.

The posterior junctional line is formed by the meeting of the pleural surfaces of the upper lobes behind the oesophagus.

The right paratracheal line is formed by the right wall of the trachea against the right lung.

The right paraspinal stripe is formed by the meeting of the right lung against the posterior mediastinal soft tissue.

Pleural fibromas tend to be asymptomatic unless large and causing symptoms related to mass effect. There is however a reasonably strong association with hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy.

The presence of haemorrhage or necrosis raises the suspicion of malignancy and although these tumours themselves are benign, around a third of them undergo malignant transformation. Surgical excision, therefore, is the usual management approach.

Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA)

In essence this is a paraneoplastic phenomenon although it can be found in many non-neoplastic circumstances. Subperiosteal new bone formation is seen as a lamellar periosteal reaction on imaging. HPOA is usually described in the distal phalanges in association with clubbing but does also occur in the rest of the appendicular skeleton. Clinically the patients experience a burning pain with swelling and stiffness of any of the affected joints.

HPOA can be caused by the presence of a bronchogenic carcinoma: this is a common scenario of medical school finals exams. Pleural fibromas are also a known cause. Extra-pulmonary causes are less common but do happen.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with atypical chest pains undergoes a cardiac MRI as part of investigations. This shows delayed hyperenhancement in an epicardial pattern.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis cardiomyopathy

Involvement of the myocardium is relatively rare in sarcoidosis. Inflammation causes myocardial scarring of the interventricular septum and left ventricle most commonly. This shows as epicardial or midwall delayed hyperenhancement on MRI. The patient in this question is certainly of an appropriate demographic for sarcoidosis. The main differential diagnoses would be myocarditis or Chagas disease based on imaging findings alone.

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy

The blood supply to the heart muscle itself is of interest here. The endocardium derives its blood directly from the chambers whereas the layer referred to as the subendocardium receives blood from the terminal branches of the coronary vessels. By the time they reach the subendocardium these blood vessels are small enough that ventricular contraction causes a degree of compression. The end result is that the subendocardium is particularly vulnerable to ischaemia, a fact which manifests in the delayed hyperenhancement patterns seen on MRI; ischaemic cardiomyopathy is seen as subendocardial delayed hyperenhancement or in more extreme cases transmural hyperenhancement. The pattern of hyperenhancement is also territorial with ischaemic cardiomyopathy, depending on which vessel(s) has been affected.

Amyloid cardiomyopathy

Amyloidosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning there is global enhancement of the endocardium, and on echocardiogram the myocardium takes on a characteristic granular and speckled appearance. In an exam question setting a history of multiple myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn disease or similar may be given to suggest secondary amyloidosis.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

HCM can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion; there are a number of specific different gene mutations which have been identified to cause cardiac myocardial hypertrophy. The most common category is asymmetrical hypertrophy, accounting for around two thirds of cases. Here the interventricular septum is markedly enlarged. stem: A 58-year-old man with multiple myeloma presents with progressive dyspnoea and peripheral oedema undergoes a cardiac MRI scan. This shows global endocardial delayed hyperenhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis cardiomyopathy

Involvement of the myocardium is relatively rare in sarcoidosis. Inflammation causes myocardial scarring of the interventricular septum and left ventricle most commonly. This shows as epicardial or midwall delayed hyperenhancement on MRI.

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy

The blood supply to the heart muscle itself is of interest here. The endocardium derives its blood directly from the chambers whereas the layer referred to as the subendocardium receives blood from the terminal branches of the coronary vessels. stem: You are reviewing the post-procedure chest radiograph for a 72-year-old lady who has just had a pacemaker inserted. There is no pneumothorax, but you notice that the positioning of the pacemaker leads indicates the patient has a left-sided SVC. You alert the clinical team and they schedule a revision procedure to correct the lead placement.
prompt: Into which structure does a left sided SVC usually drain? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Left sided SVC

This is an important but uncommon anomaly. Failure to recognise inadvertent catheterisation of a left sided SVC during pacemaker insertion can lead to arrhythmias.

90% drain into an enlarged coronary sinus

10% drain into the left atrium

Partial anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (PAPVC), scimitar syndrome

A scimitar is a curved sword such as those common in The Middle East from around the 9-10th Century onwards. It lends its name to an anomalous vein draining a hypoplastic lung as seen on CXR. In approximately half of cases the drainage is to the IVC with the remaining half draining to any one of multiple other possibilities. On the CXR the vein appears as a long tubular structure starting in the lower half of the right hemithorax and following a curved path towards the diaphragm. A scimitar vein is one component of PAPVC. The right lung drained by the vein is hypoplastic and consequently the heart is malpositioned (dextro-position) to fill the space. There is also an association with ASD.

Inter-arterial left main coronary artery

This coronary artery variant is the most significant and likely to cause symptoms. It is often repaired even if not symptomatic, but always repaired if symptomatic as there is an associated with a significant risk of sudden cardiac death. It is known as a 'malignant' course.

Hemiazygos continuation

This is a congenital anomaly usually consequent on failure of development of the infrahepatic IVC. Instead, blood below this level returns to the heart via a dilated hemiazygos vein which drains into the azygos vein at or above the level of the heart.

stem: A 31-year-old lady with a history of cystic fibrosis presents with worsening shortness of breath and a cough. She underwent a bilateral lung transplant 8 years previously. She undergoes an HRCT and you suspect she may have bronchiolitis obliterans.

explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome

There are two very similarly named syndromes which are completely different in aetiology  but frequently confused.

BOOP – bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia. This is the old term for what is now referred to as COP (Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia). There is patchy consolidation and ground glass opacification.

BOS – bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome. This is part of a CLAD (chronic lung allograft dysfunction).

In CLAD, a transplanted lung is not being rejected (another common misnomer) but the graft is undergoing fibrosis which causes respiratory dysfunction. The findings on CT, in the case of BOS, include mosaic attenuation with air trapping, bronchial wall thickening and bronchiectasis.

explanation:
Focal unilateral vocal cord uptake on a PET-CT scan is more likely to be due to the increased workload of the contralateral vocal cord muscles compensating for ipsilateral paralysis from involvement of the ipsilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve in the chest rather than metastatic infiltration of the contralateral vocal cord itself.

stem: A 78-year-old man with a productive cough, fever and malaise undergoes a CXR. He is found to have a lobar pneumonia.
prompt: What is the most likely responsible organism?
explanation:
There is considerable overlap in CXR appearances of pneumonia. Some trends can be seen but ultimately a sputum culture will lead to greater specificity. There are a number of different terms used to describe patterns that can arise.

Lobar pneumonia

The presence of bacteria in the alveoli causes oedema there. The bronchi are usually spared however; hence the presence of air bronchograms on imaging. The most common cause is streptococcus pneumonia. Klebsiella can also occur and is seen particularly in alcoholic patients or those who may be immunocompromised.

Bronchopneumonia also known as lobular pneumonia

Inflammation and oedema occurs within both the interstitium and the airways themselves giving a patchy fluffy appearance on a CXR. There is mucus plugging and volume loss (differentiating it from viral pneumonia). It occurs with staphylococcus as well as pneumococcus and klebsiella. Haemophilus would also give this appearance.

Atypical bacterial pneumonia

Sometimes bacterial infections can give rise to a pneumonia which on a CXR resembles a viral pneumonia. This occurs with mycoplasma, among others.

Viral pneumonia

Like bronchopneumonia the pathogens affect the airways and interstitium. Air trapping secondary to bronchial constriction occurs which gives rise to hyperinflation (differentiating it from bronchopneumonia). Viral pneumonias are commonly bilateral. Rhinovirus and RSV are common pathogens. Hyperinflation is a reasonably specific finding for viral pneumonias on a CXR. Appearances can be varied however with perihilar fluffy opacities or a more segmental appearance. Pleural effusions occur in around 20% of patients.

Round pneumonia

This is a specific CXR appearance which occurs in young children. Organisms such as Haemophilus, pneumococcus or streptococcus which are the usual culprits for paediatric pneumonias, are contained by the limited facility for collateral drift; the pores of Kohn have not sufficiently developed to permit spread of the bacteria and consequently the pneumonia is relatively well contained. This gives rise to a rather spherical area, usually within the posterior aspect of the lobes.

Cavitating pneumonia

Staphylococcus and streptococcus can both cause cavitation. Of the gram negative organisms, klebsiella and Haemophilus can cause cavitation.

stem: A 67-year-old lifelong smoker presents with a history of an acute onset white leg.
prompt: Which of the following is the best management plan?
options: Perform CT angiogram, start heparin, catheter directed thrombolysis +/- thrombectomy
Perform CT angiogram, start heparin, surgical bypass
Start heparin, perform CT angiogram, catheter directed thrombolysis +/- thrombectomy
Start heparin, perform CT angiogram, surgical bypass
explanation:
Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency. Management is usually decided on a case by case basis with factors such as the available technical expertise and patient comorbidity necessarily playing a part. In any case, where not contraindicated, initiating early anticoagulation can be useful and should be undertaken prior to acquiring imaging if feasible. Interventional endovascular management of the target thrombus is associated with a lower morbidity and mortality than surgical bypass or amputation although the latter may ultimately be required in some cases.

Contraindications to thrombolysis include:

Absent sensation or motor function – ie a non-viable limb

Haemorrhage

Brain tumour (due to risk of haemorrhage)

stem: A 37-year-old woman with progressive dyspnoea and cough over the last 20 months is being investigated. She has never smoked and has a history of recurrent pneumathoraces. Her CT chest shows a coarse reticulonodular interstitial pattern with multiple cysts in both lungs.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)

This is the classic description of LAM. LAM can go misdiagnosed for many years as emphysema. It occurs exclusively in non-smoking women of childbearing age, and quite often a history of spontaneous pneumothorax is given. Radiologically there are numerous small cystic spaces surrounded by normal lung. A chylous pleural effusion (negative Hounsfield units) is reasonably specific. The main differential diagnosis would be histiocytosis which tends to be associated with smoking, classically spares the costophrenic angles and gives small nodules but both can present with spontaneous pneumothorax and give small cysts. The lung volumes in LAM will remain normal whereas they can be increased in Histiocytosis (surprisingly for a fibrotic lung disease).

Histiocytosis (also known as Langerhans cell histiocytosis - LCH)

There are three separate forms of this disease:

Eosinophilic granuloma (70%) – a limited version confined to the skeleton in children or young adults. Clinically presents as fever, raised WCC and ESR with painful bony lesions. In the skull these have a typical ‘beveled edge’ or ‘hole within a hole’ appearance or can be seen as a ‘button sequestrum’. In the spine it is one of the main causes of vertebra plana.

Hand-Schüller-Christian Disease (20%) – classically a triad of destructive bony lesions, diabetes insipidus and exophthalmos. In a quarter of these patients the lungs are involved with cyst formation and spontaneous pneumothoraces possible. Nodule formation, fibrosis and honeycombing is also seen.

Letterer-Siwe Disease (10%) – a fulminant multi-organ variant affecting very young infants

There is a strong association with smoking for patients who develop pulmonary features of LCH. Heavy smoking causes an accumulation of Langerhans cells and hence, as with other inspiration-related lung diseases, there is a predilection for the upper zones. The Langerhans cells can collect with other cells and become small granulomas seen as small lung nodules. Despite being a type of fibrotic lung disease the lung volumes can be increased. Small lung cysts form and there is a risk of spontaneous pneumothorax. There is usually sparing of the costophrenic angles which can be a key finding.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)

IPF (Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) can only be diagnosed in the absence of a precipitating condition such as asbestosis, rheumatoid arthritis, or drug toxicity. Where such exists, the condition is termed UIP (Usual interstitial pneumonia). CFA (Crytpogenic fibrosing alveolitis) is a historic term for the same thing. IPF is not a true differential diagnosis for cysts since the low attenuation areas seen on CT are not true cysts (no epithelial lining is present). The macrocystic honeycombing seen is merely the consequence of the fibrotic process underlying the condition. Another clue to the diagnosis of IPF lies in the distribution; there is an apicobasilar gradient with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis affecting the lung bases and fading away superiorly.

Neurofibromatosis

Technically neurofibromatosis (type I) is included in the differential diagnosis for lung cysts (particularly when apical) however the rest of the information provided is insufficient to make this the most likely answer here.

stem: You are reviewing a cardiac MRI scan which shows a mass in the left atrium. It returns low signal on T1 and T2 images and does not enhance.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Atrial thrombus

The usual site for an atrial thrombus would be the left atrial appendage. Thrombi are not seen as mobile masses but as irregular lobulated masses. They can have a laminated appearance and the classical feature is low signal on gradient-echo MRI sequences owing to the presence of haemosiderin (blooming artefact). They do not enhance. Ventricular thrombi can form too, it is usually a sequela of a previous myocardial infarction which has healed leaving a hypomobile portion of the ventricular wall. Adjacent to that part of wall there is relative stasis sufficient to facilitate thrombus formation.

Atrial myxoma

These are the most common benign neoplasms of the heart. Although usually sporadic, they can occur as part of Carney syndrome (atrial myxoma, facial/buccal pigmentation, sertoli tumours of the testis and multiple other findings. Not to be confused with Carney triad - pulmonary hamartomas, gastric leiomyosarcomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas). The finding of a small mass attached to the interatrial septum by a stalk is classical. Their mobility allows some to prolapse through the relevant atrioventricular valve during the cardiac cycle. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for the more common left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided myxomas. Iso or hypointensity on T1w MRI is typical.

Carney Triad

Carney Syndrome

1. Pulmonary harmatoma

Atrial myxoma

2. Gastric leiomyosarcoma (GIST)

Facial/ buccal pigmentation

3. Extra-adrenal paraganglioma

Sertoli tumour of the testis

Pituitary adenoma

Papillary fibroelastoma

These tumours are rare even for cardiac tumours but yet are the most common cardiac tumour to be associated with the valves. Rather counter-intuitively, they do not cause valvular dysfunction. They are usually quite small and, like myxomas, relatively mobile, attached by a stalk, and able to prolapse through a valve but where myxomas usually arise from the interatrial septum, papillary fibroelastomas grow from the valve itself. Histopathologically they are gelatinous tumours resembling sea anemones with multiple papillary projections. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided masses. On MRI they are often low in signal on T2 weighted sequences owing to their fibrous nature.

Cardiac sarcoma

There are many different types of cardiac sarcoma. Cardiac sarcomas are the most common cause of primary malignant cardiac tumours. Their presentation usually relates either to embolic phenomena such as TIAs or symptoms from invasion such as pericardial effusion. In contrast to myxomas or fibroelastomas, malignant lesions tend to have a broad attachment to the heart wall. Another useful differentiating feature on imaging is the involvement of more than one chamber of the heart.

Cardiac metastases

Metastases are significantly more common than cardiac sarcomas meaning metastases are the most common malignant cardiac tumours. In contrast to myxomas or fibroelastomas, malignant lesions tend to have a broad attachment to the heart wall. Tumours can be from lung or breast cancer, lymphoma, leukaemia and malignant melanoma.

stem: Which of the following features if noted on a CT abdominal angiogram would render an abdominal aortic aneurysm unsuitable for a standard endovascular repair?
prompt: Select one answer only.
explanation:
For the most part it will be the vascular surgeons or interventional radiologists themselves who decide on a case-by-case basis whether they themselves are prepared to attempt endovascular repair of a given aneurysm. Broadly speaking however, there are a number of criteria which the surgeon or interventionalist would be wise to abide by:

Distance to the renal arteries – 10mm used to be the absolute minimum landing zone distance required but many of the grafts would required a minimum of 15mm. If the landing zone is less than 10mm a fenestrated graft must be used to preserve the patency of the renal arteries.

Angle of the neck – this is measured one of two ways in the literature. Consequently there are two different values for an acceptable angle. A purely straight aneurysm would have a neck angle of either 180o or 0o in each of the different measuring systems. Thus the acceptable neck cut-off values are 120o or 60o in each case.

Angle of the common iliac artery – fortunately this is easier to remember. Iliac arteries at 90o or worse are significantly harder to stent. Further consideration is usually given to the overall tortuosity of the iliac arteries but this relates to endovascular access as opposed to stent deployment.

Common iliac artery (CIA) length – Ideally the CIA should be longer than 20mm to accommodate the stents used. Shorter lengths may require landing in the external iliac artery with deliberate occlusion of the internal iliac artery and reliance on pelvic collaterals.

Common iliac artery diameter – Stents are difficult to place where the diameter of the CIA is less than 7mm.

stem: A 78-year-old lady has a new diagnosis of lung cancer. There is a 3cm mass lesion touching the left main bronchus in the left upper lobe. No chest wall invasion is seen but there is a second smaller lesion in the apex of the right upper lobe. Enlarged lymph nodes are seen in the contralateral hilar lymph nodes. There is a pleural effusion which, when tapped and examined for cytology reveals malignant cells. An adrenal lesion is seen on the lowest slices of the chest phase which enhances strongly with contrast. On the portal venous phase of the abdomen the lesion remains hyperattenuating.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT considered as metastatic?
explanation:
Contralateral hilar lymph nodes denote N3 disease.

In an ideal world every trainee radiologist would have all the intricacies of staging for all tumour types committed to memory. A qualified subspecialist radiologist could reasonably be expected to be extremely familiar with the staging for cancers within their remit but for the majority of trainees it is simply not practical to memorise each and every staging scheme. As an overall strategy, the most important stages to understand are those which change the management for patients. Of note with lung cancer, at Stage IIIb the management changes significantly because stage IIIb and stage IV patients are unresectable. Another useful facet to lung cancer (TNM) staging is satellite nodules:

Same lobe = T3

Different lobe = T4

Contralateral lung = M1

For lung cancer some of the important staging features are as follows:

T1 tumours are <3cm

N1 = ipsilateral hilar nodes

T2 tumours are between 3-5cm or involve the main bronchus, the visceral pleura, or have atelectasis which reaches the hilum.

N2 = ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal nodes

T3 tumours are 5-7cm or have extension to:

Chest wall

Pleura or pericardium

<2cm of the carina

Satellite nodules within the same lobe

N3 = contralateral hilar, mediastinal or supraclavicular nodes

M1 = bilateral lesions, malignant pleural effusion, distant metastases

T4 tumours are >7cm or affect diaphragm, mediastinal organs, carina, vertebral body

T1 and T2 both have further subdivisions.

Unresectable tumours are T4, N3 or M1.

Beyond TNM staging patients with similar prognostic outcomes are given further stages. Simple observation of these groupings reveals the following:

Stage I patients MUST be N0

Stage III patients MUST have a sum ≥ 3 (ie T2N2M0, or T1N2M0). [NB some patients with Stage II will also have a sum of 3 (for example T2N1M0) however ALL stage III patients have a sum ≥ 3.]

Stage IIIb patients are unresectable → stage IIIb is denoted either by N3 status or T4N2.

stem: A 67-year-old man develops a swollen, tender, pulsatile mass in his right groin two days after a diagnostic cardiac angiogram. He undergoes an ultrasound which demonstrates a 2.5cm pseudoaneurysm of the profunda femoris artery.
prompt: What is the most appropriate next management?
options: Conservative management with repeat USS in 48hrs
explanation:
Approximately 1-2% of cardiac catheterizations are complicated by femoral pseudoaneurysm formation. An iatrogenic pseudoaneurysm forms when there is contained leakage of blood from a vessel puncture site. The sac of blood communicates with the lumen and continuous flow within the pseudoaneurysm prevents clot formation. Pseudoaneurysms pose a significant risk of rupture with potentially catastrophic consequences if they do. Risk factors for pseudoaneurysm formation include:

Patient related

Anticoagulation

Haemodialysis

Calcified arteries

Obesity

Procedural

Low puncture sites (SFA or profunda femoris)

Suboptimal post-procedure pressure

Some aneurysms do spontaneously thrombose. Ultrasound follow up is not completely unreasonable as a management technique where further intervention is relatively or absolutely contra-indicated, and with appropriate patient counselling regarding risks.

Small pseudoaneurysms (<2cm diameter) can usually be managed non-invasively with manual compression. The goal of manual compression is to occlude the neck of the pseudoaneurysm. This causes stasis within the sac and facilitates clotting. USS is a useful adjunct to compression.

Larger pseudoaneurysms are often amenable to occlusion via ultrasound guided thrombin injection. The average size for pseudoaneurysms amenable to thrombin injection is around 3cm diameter. Larger pseudoaneuryms can be managed with thrombin but It is only safe to perform this if manual compression during the injection is able to satisfactorily occlude the neck of the aneurysm to prevent thrombin embolising distally. Thrombin injection can be used even for patients undergoing anticoagulation with heparin or warfarin and even for higher pseudoaneurysms of the groin region, above the inguinal ligament.

For pseudoaneurysms not amenable to either of these two management strategies surgical ligation would be the next option. Endovascular stenting is not usually performed for femoral pseudoaneurysms owing to the risk of kink formation within the stent on hip flexion. Endovascular coiling is also unsuitable for femoral pseudoaneurysms as the femoral artery is an inexpendable vessel; coiling it would risk leg ischaemia.

stem: You are reviewing the chest radiograph of a young adult who presented to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath. There is left sided increased transradiance.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
There is a differential diagnosis for unilateral hypertransradiancy.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Poland syndrome

This is a congenital condition where there is hypoplasia or aplasia of the pectoralis major muscle on one side in association with abnormalities in the ipsilateral hand such as syndactyly, and hypoplasia of the middle phalanx. The absence of the large pectoralis major muscle is seen on a chest radiograph as abnormal hyperlucency on the affected side.

stem: A 21-year-old man with a significant family history of sudden cardiac death presents with collapse. An electrocardiogram performed in the Emergency Department demonstrates a left bundle branch block. An echocardiogram demonstrates a dilated right ventricle. A cardiac MRI scan is performed which identifies high T1 and T2 signal in the thickened right ventricular free wall. Fat-saturated sequences show signal loss within the right ventricular wall. The left ventricle appears normal.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC)

There is a familial preponderance in around 50% of cases. Resultant arrhythmias are usually LBBB or ventricular tachycardia. There is fibro-fatty degeneration of the right ventricular wall as well as right ventricular dilatation.

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

This is characterised by non-dilated thickening of the ventricular wall. If it is associated with left ventricular outflow obstruction, it can have a grave prognosis. This is due to a venturi effect pulling the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve into the outflow tract (SAM - systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve).

Sarcoidosis

Usually gives high T2 signal in the midwall, affecting predominantly the septal base. It can mimic focal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to focal wall thickening from oedema. It does not tend to affect the right ventricle.

Amyloidosis

Diffuse subendocardial gadolinium enhancement and diffusely increased T1 myocardial signal are the classical features.

Cardiac myxoma

Myxomas commonly affect the atrium (left atrium usually). They are the most common cardiac primary tumour in adults. They are usually attached the inter-atrial septum and demonstrate post-gadolinium enhancement.

stem: You are reviewing the abdominal radiograph of a 70-year-old woman who presented with acute severe abdominal pain. This shows obscuration of the psoas shadow with lateral shifting of the perinephric stripe. She goes on to have a CT scan.
prompt: Which ONE of the following is NOT a sign of impending aortic aneurysm rupture?
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a sign of impending aortic aneurysm rupture.

Obscuration of the psoas shadow occurs in de facto rupture, not pending rupture.

Detecting an aneurysm on an abdominal radiograph is unusual and requires a high degree of clinical suspicion. Owing to the presence of blood in the retroperitoneum adjacent to the psoas muscles, a ruptured aneurysm can obscure the psoas shadow and shift the kidney laterally.

Rupture and impending rupture

On a CT scan the diagnosis is often obvious with a significant amount of peri-aortic fat stranding, a large volume of retroperitoneal blood and frank contrast extravasation. In acutely pending cases, there are a number of signs which point to the diagnosis:

Crescenteric high attenuation on an unenhanced scan - acute mural thrombus is strongly associated with rupture

Focal discontinuity of calcified intima / tangential calcium sign - where the intimal calcification appears to point away (in a tangent) from the expected circumferential course

Draped aorta - the posterior contour of the aorta follows that of the adjacent vertebral body

An aortic aneurysm is simply a dilatation of the aorta. The vast majority of these will be degenerate, caused by longstanding atherosclerosis and hypertension. Connective tissue diseases such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos can predispose to aortic aneurysms at an earlier age. Fusiform aneurysmal dilatation is typical of a degenerate aneurysm.

The national screening program currently screens men aged 65 using ultrasound. The risk age group is men aged 65-80 and anyone with a family history of a first degree relative with an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

Thus men older than 65, women with a family history and men younger than 65 with a family history are all also screened outside of the national screening programme if they are referred by a GP. Aneurysms are also picked up incidentally during abdominal scanning for any other reason, on USS and non-USS modalities.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Hodgkin lymphoma

Lipoma

Malignant germ cell tumour

Malignant thymoma

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma

A 61-year-old lady with a fatigue and weakness after minimal exertion undergoes a CXR which shows a widened mediastinum. A subsequent CT shows a lobulated 8cm anterior mediastinal mass with pleural deposits.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The ‘5Ts’ of anterior mediastinal masses are a useful aide memoire:

Thymoma

Thyroid tumours

Teratoma

Thoracic aorta

Terrible lymphoma

Malignant thymoma

These tumours spread by invading the mediastinum and encasing the lung with pleural thickening. Vascular invasion is also seen. There is an association with myasthenia gravis, hence the features of weakness and fatigue symptoms with lid lag and diplopia also commonly described. Pleural deposits are also a good feature to suggest a malignant thymoma over some of the other possible options.

Hodgkin lymphoma

Hodgkin lymphoma has two age peaks in prevalence, one in the late 20s and one in the late 70s. It can present at any age however. If a histological finding of Reed-Sternberg cells (binucleate white cells) is given there can be no other diagnosis. Hodgkin lymphoma tends to cause anterior mediastinal masses whereas Non-hodgkin lymphoma tends to cause posterior mediastinal masses. Hodgkin lymphoma nodal involvement spreads contiguously from one region to the next. This makes the staging very easy to remember.

Stage I = one nodal group involved

Stage II = two or more nodal groups involved on the same side of the diaphragm

Stage III = nodal groups on either side of the diaphragm

Stage IV = involvement of non-lymphatic structures (e.g. bone or lung)

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL)

NHL is 4 times more prevalent than Hodgkin lymphoma. Thoracic lymph node enlargement is common and classically affects the posterior mediastinum. Unlike Hodgkin lymphoma, NHL demonstrates non-contiguous spread and thus the whole neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis should be included in staging imaging.

The following table summarises some of the imaging features separating the two diagnoses:

Hodgkin lymphoma

Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

Mediastinal nodes

Anterior

Posterior

Spread

Contiguous

Non-contiguous

Predominantly

Thorax

Abdomen

→ Abdominal involvement

Approx 4%

>50%

→ Thoracic involvement

Approx 85%

Approx 50%

Malignant germ cell tumour

These include seminomas and non-seminomatous (embryonal, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma, mixed cell type) tumours. Generally speaking they affect young adults and an elevated hCG, LDH, or alpha fetoprotein is usually present. The presence of effusions suggests local pleural invasion and may well be seen. Although the presence or absence of calcification is not featured in this question, the lack of calcification is in-keeping with seminomatous tumours.

Lipoma

Lipomas are usually easily distinguished by their fat content, giving negative Hounsfield units. No Hounsfield units have been provided here but the remainder of the clinical information provided would not be explained by a lipoma.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with chest pain after exertion. He undergoes a cardiac CT scan to investigate for coronary artery disease.
prompt: Which of the following anatomical variants, if present, is most significant and may be causing the symptoms?
options: Anomalous left coronary artery arising from the pulmonary artery
Anomalous right coronary artery arising from the left coronary cusp
Myocardial bridging of the left coronary artery
explanation:
Inter-arterial left main coronary artery

This variant is the most significant and likely to cause symptoms. It is often repaired even if not symptomatic, but always repaired if symptomatic as there is an associated with a significant risk of sudden cardiac death.

Anomalous right coronary artery arising from the left coronary cusp

This variant is rarely symptomatic and is usually only repaired if symptomatic.

Myocardial bridging of the left anterior descending artery

This describes a short portion of the left anterior descending artery which dives within the myocardium. It can occasionally be symptomatic.

Anomalous left coronary artery arising from the pulmonary artery

This variant can result in symptoms due to reversal of flow in the left coronary artery when pulmonary artery pressure decreases. This is also known as ‘steal’ syndrome. This variant is usually fatal in early childhood.

Coronary fistula

This occurs when a connection between a coronary artery and cardiac chamber or great vessels. It can result in large coronary artery aneurysms.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with severe abdominal pain which is constant, epigastric and radiates through to the back. A CT scan is performed which shows she has a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm.
prompt: Which of the following branches of the abdominal aorta is a paired visceral artery? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The abdominal aorta is the largest artery in the abdominal cavity. It arises as a continuation of the thoracic aorta as it passes posterior to the median arcuate ligament of the diaphragm at the T12 vertebral level.

It descends caudally in the retroperitoneal space, anterior and to the left of the lumbar vertebral bodies and to the left of the inferior vena cava.

It is approximately 13 cm long and ends slightly to the left of the midline at the L4 vertebral level where it bifurcates into the right and left common iliac arteries.

The abdominal aorta has three main groups of branches:

1. Single ventral gut arteries:

Coeliac artery (T12) – supplies the stomach, abdominal oeseophagus, liver, spleen, superior pancreas, and superior duodenum

Superior mesenteric artery (L1) – supplies the distal duodenum, jejunum. Ileum, ascending colon and part of the transverse colon

Inferior mesenteric artery (L3) – supplies the large intestine from the splenic flexure to the upper part of the rectum

2. Paired visceral arteries:

Middle adrenal arteries (L1) – supply the adrenal glands

Renal arteries (L2) – supply the kidneys

Gonadal arteries (L2/L3) – supply the testicles/ovaries

3. Paired wall arteries:

Inferior phrenic arteries (T12) – supply the diaphragm

Four paired lumbar arteries (between L1 and L4) – supply the abdominal wall and spinal cord

It also gives off one single unpaired parietal artery, the median sacral artery, at the L4 vertebral level.

The abdominal aorta, its relations and branches (from Gray’s Anatomy)

stem: A 67-year-old man is having a cardiac MRI for investigation of exertional dyspnoea. The radiographer explains to you that the images are degraded by an RF artifact.
prompt: How is this likely to have affected the image?
explanation:
Physics questions should be covered in the FRCR part 1 but every so often one can crop up. Fortunately they are far more clinical than the physics exam, covering problems that a radiologist might face on real scans.

Problems with the RF pulses can cause a number of different problems. Chief among them is inhomogeneous fat suppression because the 90o pulses applied in order to suppress the fat signal become slightly more or less than 90o in areas, thereby incompletely suppressing the fat signal.

Wrap around artifact occurs when the field of view is too small.

Ghosting in the phase encoding direction occurs either due to patient motion or blood flow in large vessels.

Truncation artifact causes Gibbs ringing and occurs due to the production of a digital signal from analogue signals superimposed on one another but curtailed for practical purposes (an exact digital signal would require an infinite number of analogue signals).

The india ink phenomenon is caused by chemical shift artifact

stem: You are reviewing an MRI scan of a 45-year-old woman who recently underwent a successful uterine artery embolisation for management of menorrhagia.
prompt: Which of the following is a complication of this procedure? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Asherman syndrome

Historically this condition was the result of infection with tuberculosis but nowadays it is more often the consequence of iatrogenic endometrial damage. The formation of intrauterine synechiae leads to subfertility and these fibrous bands can be seen on HSG as filling defects and surface irregularity. Asherman syndrome should not occur following uterine artery embolisation.

In the world of interventional radiology, uterine fibroid embolisation is gaining momentum. The uterine artery arises from the internal iliac artery whereas the ovarian artery arises directly from the aorta and its branches have a corkscrew appearance on angiography. Anastomoses between the two arteries or the two sides exist in approximately 20% of patients. Patients should be counselled for the risk of ovarian dysfunction subsequent to the procedure and patients over the age of 45 are at particular risk. Pedunculated fibroids are said to be poor candidates for embolisation owing to their propensity to detach however the literature is slightly contradictory on this topic.

Following a successful embolisation the fibroid should undergo infarction and involution. On an MRI scan initially there will be high T1 signal with low T2 signal and no enhancement of the infarcted tissue post-contrast. As the fibroid liquifies, from around 3 months onwards post-procedure, the T2 signal becomes brighter.

Complications include:

Infections (Endometritis, PID and TOA)

DVT / PE - due to compression of pelvic veins by enlarged uterus (therefore a complication of the underlying pathology as opposed to the procedure itself)

Ovarian dysfunction - increased risk >45years due to greater propensity for uterine-ovarian artery anastomoses. Careful examination of pre-procedure MR angiography images helps reduce this risk

Fibroid passage

Haemorrhage

Uterine necrosis - look for lack of endometrial enhancement

Meig syndrome

This is a triad of an ovarian fibroma (usually, other ovarian tumours do cause it too), ascites and pleural effusions. A right sided pleural effusion is more common than the left. The underlying mechanism is unclear. Two possible explanations are that either the tumour irritates the peritoneum leading to a build-up of inflammatory fluid, or that histamine release alongside other chemicals and hormones causes vasodilation and fluid exudation that way.

stem: A 30-year-old man with Marfan syndrome develops sudden onset, severe chest pain. A CT scan is performed, which reveals a diagnosis of aortic dissection.
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the aorta is FALSE?
options: The aortic arch commences at the point of the pericardial reflection on the aorta
The aortic arch commences posterior to the manubriosternal joint at the level of the third costal cartilage
The descending aorta commences at the level of the intervertebral disc between the 4th and 5th thoracic vertebrae
The left aortic sinus contains the origin of the left coronary artery
The left common carotid artery arises at the mid point of the manubrium sterni
explanation:
The aorta receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and delivers it to the body. It can be divided into three parts:

The ascending aorta

The arch of the aorta

The descending aorta

The ascending aorta commences at the opening of the aortic valve in the left ventricle of the heart. It runs through a common pericardial sheath with the pulmonary trunk. The ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk twist around each other, with the aorta initially lying posterior to the pulmonary trunk, before twisting to the right and lying anteriorly to it.

At the root of the ascending aorta, the lumen contains three aortic sinuses. The left aortic sinus contains the origin of the left coronary artery and the right aortic sinus contains the right coronary artery. Together these two arteries supply the heart. The third sinus, which is called the posterior aortic sinus, does not give rise to a coronary artery.

The aortic arch commences at the point of the pericardial reflection on the aorta, which is posterior to the manubriosternal joint at the level of the second costal cartilage. It passes posterior and to the left, over the left main bronchus and ends at the left side of the body of the 4th thoracic vertebra. Its highest level is the mid point of the manubrium sterni and it is at this level that its three main branches arise:

Brachiocephalic artery, which supplies blood to the brain, head, and right side of the thorax

Left common carotid artery, which supplies blood to the left side of the head and neck

Left subclavian artery, which supplies blood to the left side of the thorax

The descending aorta commences at the end of the arch of the aorta, which is at the level of the intervertebral disc between the 4th and 5th thoracic vertebrae. The descending aorta, in turn, becomes then thoracic and abdominal aorta.

The aorta and its three main branches

stem: An 82-year-old man is recovering from a severe community-acquired pneumonia and acute kidney injury. During his recovery, he develops a small amount of malaena. He is haemodynamically stable but the malaena has persisted over the course of the last two days.
prompt: What is the best next investigation for him?
explanation: In the setting of a smaller district general hospital it is unlikely that nuclear medicine tests or interventional radiological options would be available and even in some larger hospitals the service may be restricted to office hours. In such cases it is highly likely that the patient would receive a CT scan and/or a colonoscopy. Colonoscopy is generally considered to be the first line management for the investigation of lower GI bleeding and an OGD would be the first line investigation for upper GI bleeding although this has not been provided as an option. The question refers to malena and without further information this would be taken (in an exam question setting) as a reference to an upper GI source. CT angiography can localize bleeding points when there is approximately 0.35ml/min of blood loss. This compares with approximately 0.1ml/min capabilities of Tc-99m labeled red blood cell scans. Accurate localization is, however, significantly higher with a CT angiogram than with the nuclear medicine test and the latter should not be performed in unstable patients or those with ongoing fresh bleeding per rectum. A recent history or ongoing acute kidney injury does not make this patient an ideal candidate for CT angiography. Surgery may yet be on this patient’s cards but there are a few options to explore prior to the need for surgery.

stem: Which of the following would be a contraindication to catheter directed thrombolysis in the context of an acute ischaemic limb?
prompt: Select one option only.
explanation:
Some of the prominent contraindications to thrombolysis are:

Major trauma at presentation

Lumbar puncture within the last 1 week

Surgery or CPR within the last 2 weeks

Upper GI bleed within the last 3 weeks

CVA within the last 8 weeks

Bleeding disorder

INR > 1.6

Frequency is not a helpful term.

Incidence (annual)                    =          the number of new cases per year in a population

Prevalence                                 =          the overall number of cases in a population

We can assume we are approaching such questions from the radiologist's perspective, namely when reporting a CT chest of a patient with no known primary, if there are lung metastases from where are they most likely to have come? It is therefore necessary to consider how prevalent a disease is in the whole population, as well as how often metastasis occurs for each cancer itself. For example you may be studying a cancer which very commonly metastasizes to the lungs and comparing it with one that rarely does so but if the former is incredibly rare and the later extremely common then the so-called frequency of lung metastasis may not be obvious.

stem: A 25-year-old woman develops worsening calf pain and swelling. She has been treated for deep vein thrombosis previously but anticoagulation was discontinued following 6 months of treatment. She has no other pro-thrombotic risk factors. A CT is performed and confirms an underlying problem.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
May-Thurner Syndrome

This condition causes recurrent left leg swelling and left sided deep vein thrombosis due to obstruction of the left common iliac vein where it is crossed by the right common iliac artery. The vein is compressed between the right CIA and the spine. Patients can also develop pelvic varicosities and collateral pathways connecting left and right to allow drainage of the pelvic organs via the contralateral side.

prompt: What is the correct dose to administer?

Adrenaline 1:1000 0.5mL IV, with repeat bolus of 1mL if no response
Adrenaline 1:1000 0.5ml IM, 10mg hydrocortisone IV (or IM), 200mg of chlorphenamine IV (or IM)
Adrenaline 1:1000 0.5ml IM, with repeat 0.5mL bolus if no response
Adrenaline 1:1000 1ml IM with repeat bolus of 1.5mL if no response
explanation:
The recommended management of anaphylaxis has changed.

Initial management involves removing any triggers, and lying the patient flat (or on left side if pregnant).

IM adrenaline is then used:

Child 6-12y - 300 micrograms (0.3mL of 1:1000)

Young child 6m-6y - 150 micrograms (0.15mL of 1:1000)

Adrenaline - 0.5ml of 1:10,000 IV or 1:1000 IM

prompt: Which of these is the LEAST likely cause?
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the LEAST likely option.

All of the answers above can cause mosaic attenuation. Mosaic attenuation describes the appearance of the lungs on an HRCT where the underlying pathology has affected different parts of the lung to different degrees and consequently the lungs appear heterogeneous in attenuation, as though made up of different tiles fitting together, like a mosaic. It can be difficult to determine whether it is the darker areas or the more attenuating areas which represent the abnormal areas of lung.

There is a differential diagnosis for mosaic attenuation of the lung but broadly speaking the causes fall into one of three categories:

Parenchymal disease – the abnormal areas are high in attenuation and appear as ground glass opacification.

Poor ventilation – the abnormal areas are low in attenuation, these are areas where perfusion has reduced in reaction to poor ventilation.

Mosaic perfusion (also known as mosaic oligaemia) – the abnormal areas are low in attenuation, these are areas where perfusion has been impeded by a vascular pathology such as CTEPH (Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension)

stem: A 34-year-old man undergoes a left pneumonectomy for lung cancer. He recovers well post-operatively and is reviewed in clinic six months later. He has been reasonably well but has developed increasing breathlessness more recently. A CXR shows mediastinal shift to the left and a near complete white out of the left hemithorax.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The patient has developed post-pneumonectomy syndrome. The contralateral lung has hyperexpanded, pushing the mediastinum to the ipsilateral side to surgery and leading to respiratory compromise.

Overall post-pneumonectomy changes are features of volume loss with fluid accumulation in the affected hemithorax. A pleural effusion is therefore an expected finding in post-pneumonectomy patients. A unilateral effusion in patients who haven't had a lung resected would be expected to cause contralateral (not ipsilateral as in the vignette) mediastinal shift, if anything.

As the now empty hemithorax gradually fills with fluid an air-fluid level is to be expected. This should reach approximately half-way up the chest on a CXR by day 4 or day 5 and should reach at least 66%, if not 100%, of the height of the chest on a CXR after a fortnight. Ipsilateral mediastinal shift also usually takes place owing to the volume loss although this is not an absolute finding; Some patients will have no mediastinal shift. Diaphragmatic elevation would be an expected finding, diaphragmatic flattening would not.

Post-operative complications of a pneumonectomy include:

5-10% bronchopulmonary fistula

Contralateral tracheal shift

Reduction in height of the fluid level on sequential films

5% ARDS

5% Pulmonary oedema

<5% empyema

Post-pneumonectomy syndrome

This occurs when hyperexpansion of the remaining lung displaces the heart, with rotation of the heart in an anticlockwise fashion along its long axis.

This develops in the first year and usually affects young adults or children. Patients develop exertional dyspnoea or recurrent infections

prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the bronchi is true?
options: The left main bronchus is more vertical than the right main bronchus
The left main bronchus passes superior to the arch of the aorta
The right main bronchus is longer than the left main bronchus
There are two secondary bronchi on the right
The tertiary bronchi supply the bronchopulmonary segments
explanation:
The left main bronchus is thinner but longer than the right. It is typically 5 cm long and enters the left lung opposite the 6th thoracic vertebra. It passes beneath the arch of the aorta and crosses in front of the oesophagus, the thoracic duct and the descending aorta.

The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left. It is typically 2.5 cm long and enters the right lung opposite the 5th thoracic vertebra.

stem: A 45-year-old lady is being investigated for atypical chest pains which she has been experiencing for the last two months. She is worried as she has a strong family history of heart problems. She undergoes a 24-hour ECG which is normal, but an exercise ECG shows some lateral T-wave inversion.
prompt: Which of the following is the next best test to perform? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
This lady is showing some signs of myocardial ischaemia during exercise. The best modality to image this and demonstrates the extent of the territory involved would therefore be a stressed test. The best test for this would be an adenosine stress MRI.

Adenosine stress MRI has overtaken dobutamine stress MRI in terms of sensitivity and specificity for investigating the presence of ischaemia or infarction. Adenosine causes coronary vasodilation. If there is a haemodynamically significant stenosis to a coronary vessel, the vessels distal to the stenosis are already maximally dilated to maximise flow and thus the application of adenosine makes no difference to the vessel calibre or the resultant perfusion. Furthermore, the vasodilatation to the remaining unoccluded vessels can 'steal' blood from the stenosed territory and this is seen as hypoperfusion to the affected territory. Dipyridamole (antiplatelet), blocks uptake of adenosine and so patients taking this are also poor candidates for this test, however dipyridimole itself can also induce vasodilatation so may be used as an agent in its own right instead of adenosine.

Contraindications to adenosine include:

Second or third degree heart block

Bronchospasm

Hypotension <90mmHg systolic

Myocardial infarction within 48hrs

Uncontrolled arrhythmia

Severe/critical aortic stenosis

The half-life of adenosine is exceptionally short, around 10 seconds, thus any side effects experienced during the scan resolve very quickly. It also means that during the scan, in order to maintain the effect, the adenosine must be given as an infusion.

Dobutamine stress MRI used to be used but has largely been superseded by adenosine stress MRIs. Dobutamine is a sympathomimetic so works by inducing the heart to beat both faster and stronger. By increasing the stress on the whole heart, hitherto compensated areas are unmasked. The drug is given at increasing doses ever 3 minutes until any of:

The heart rate has increased to around 85% of its resting maximum

New wall motion abnormality is seen

Blood pressure rises above 240/220mmHg

Systolic blood pressure falls by 40mmHg

The patient develops persistent arrhythmias

The patient becomes too symptomatic to continue the scan

Aside from the usual contra-indications to performing the MRI in the first place, specific contra-indications to performing a dobutamine stress MRI include:

Hypertension >220/120mmHg

Unstable angina

Aortic stenosis (severe)

Uncontrolled atrial fibrillation

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Congestive heart failure

A stress echocardiogram is particularly useful for further investigating patients in whom a stress ECG was inconclusive. Many patients are unable to tolerate the physical demands (treadmill) of a stress ECG. Patients are given dobutamine, much like for a stress cardiac MRI study. Wall-motion abnormalities can be seen, as with cardiac MRI, and these correspond to areas of non-viable or hibernating myocardium and provide targets for revascularisation. An echocardiogram has the obvious advantages of lower cost, wider availability and faster scanning time than an MRI. The contra-indications to this test are the same as those for cardiac MRI.

Cardiac CT is indicated for acute cardiac or major vessel pathology as it is quick and more readily available than MRI. It can be used to assess the calcium-score of the coronary arteries as well as patency/occlusions to identify targets for acute revascularisation. It is also useful for quantifying aneurysmal dilatation of the aortic root.

An invasive angiogram is also indicated for acute ischaemic cardiac pathology, particularly in the presence of ECG changes suggesting an acute myocardial infarction. Ideally this can then lead to endovascular stenting or clot-retrieval to open up the target artery. The procedure is obviously not without risk but can be life-saving, and is still considered as the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery stenosis however the fact of stenosis does not provide information on the effect of the underlying myocardium. In the acute scenario it is reasonable to assume that a stenosed vessel is the cause of the symptoms, but the picture is less straightforward in sub-acute or chronic chest pains.

stem: A 75-year-old woman attends for an outpatient appointment with her rheumatologist. She develops atypical chest pains and is admitted for an ECHO. The cardiologist notices a speckled granular appearance to the myocardium. She goes on to have an MRI which shows global subendocardial delayed hyperenhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Amyloid cardiomyopathy

Amyloidosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning there is global enhancement of the endocardium, and on echocardiogram the myocardium takes on a characteristic granular and speckled appearance. In an exam question setting a history of multiple myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease or similar may be given to suggest secondary amyloidosis.

Sarcoidosis cardiomyopathy

Involvement of the myocardium is relatively rare in sarcoidosis. Inflammation causes myocardial scarring of the interventricular septum and left ventricle most commonly. This shows as epicardial or midwall delayed hyperenhancement on MRI.

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy

The blood supply to the heart muscle itself is of interest here. The endocardium derives its blood directly from the chambers whereas the layer referred to as the subendocardium receives blood from the terminal branches of the coronary vessels. By the time they reach the subendocardium these blood vessels are small enough that ventricular contraction causes a degree of compression. The end result is that the subendocardium is particularly vulnerable to ischaemia, a fact which manifests in the delayed hyperenhancement patterns seen on MRI; ischaemic cardiomyopathy is seen as subendocardial delayed hyperenhancement or in more extreme cases transmural hyperenhancement. The pattern of hyperenhancement is also territorial with ischaemic cardiomyopathy, depending on which vessel(s) has been affected.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

HCM can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion; there are a number of specific different gene mutations which have been identified to cause cardiac myocardial hypertrophy. The most common category is asymmetrical hypertrophy, accounting for around two thirds of cases. Here the interventricular septum is markedly enlarged. The remaining third of cases display symmetrical/concentric hypertrophy or apical hypertrophy. Patients are younger than most of those with ischaemic cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning midwall hyperenhancement at the junction between the right and left ventricles is typical.

Alcoholic cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy occurs in patients with a history of alcohol abuse. There is dilation of both ventricles alongside thinning of the myocardium which appears hypokinetic on dynamic studies. Myocardial fibrosis occurs and because this typically affects the mid-myocardium it can be differentiated from ischaemic cardiomyopathy which is often transmural and confined to vascular territories. The different areas show delayed enhancement on MRI scans.

explanation:
Cardiac CT is susceptible to artefact in multiple forms.

Streak artefact can be caused by metallic artefacts, severe calcification within the coronary arteries and also a high density of contrast within the SVC or right atrium.

Bleeding is common to both conditions as are pleural effusions is common to both which leaves pulmonary oedema. This is usually florrid in an amniotic fluid embolus and readily appreciable on a chest radiograph.

Amniotic fluid embolus

This is thankfully a very rare complication of pregnancy since it has a very high mortality rate. Amniotic fluid entering the venous system causes a huge anaphylactoid reaction and DIC. Many of the patients succumb too rapidly for imaging to play any role. Where patients are imaged however, the features are those of adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) / pulmonary oedema with bilateral diffuse ground glass opacification. Unlike usual pulmonary emboli, amniotic fluid emboli is not seen as a filling defect on CTPA and it would be highly unlikely that the patient would be stable enough to undergo a VQ scan.

HELLP syndrome

Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets.

This condition occurs in the perinatal peri-partum period an manifests as right upper quadrant pain and tenderness with subcutaneous oedema, effusions and ascites. Imaging does not play a significant role in the management of this condition unless to rule out other causes of the symptoms which have developed.

explanation:
The ribs are narrow, curved, flat bones that form most of the thoracic cage.

The true ribs are the first seven ribs (sometimes eight). They are called the true ribs because they attach the vertebrae to the sternum through their costal cartilages.

The false ribs are the 8th to the 10th ribs (the vertebrochondral ribs). They are called the false ribs because their cartilages are joined to the cartilage of the rib just superior to them.

The floating ribs are the 11th and 12th ribs. They are called the floating ribs because their cartilages end in the posterior abdominal musculature.

prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the nerve supply of the lungs is true?
options: The lungs contain no pain conducting fibres
The parasympathetic fibres are derived from the phrenic nerve
The parasympathetic fibres stimulate vasoconstriction of the pulmonary vessels
The sympathetic fibres stimulate relaxation of the bronchial smooth muscle
The visceral afferent fibres conduct pain impulses to the sensory ganglion of the phrenic nerve
explanation:
The nerve supply of the lungs is derived from the pulmonary plexuses and features sympathetic, parasympathetic, and visceral afferent fibres:

The parasympathetic fibres of the lungs are derived from the vagus nerve. These serve to stimulate secretion from the bronchial glands, contraction of the bronchial smooth muscle, and vasodilatation of the pulmonary vessels.

The sympathetic fibres of the lungs are derived from the sympathetic trunks. These serve to stimulate relaxation of the bronchial smooth muscle, and vasoconstriction of the pulmonary vessels.

The visceral afferent fibres of the lung conduct pain impulses to the sensory ganglion of the vagus nerve.

In patients with heart rates below around 70 beats per minute, end-diastole is the optimal time for imaging. In these patients, diastole is the longest period the heart is still for, and therefore ideal for imaging.

Diastole is also the part of the cardiac cycle which decreases in duration when the heart rate increases. This reduces the duration of the imaging window during cardiac CT. The period of time the heart remains still for in systole stays constant when the heart rate increases. Therefore in patients with increased heart rates, imaging at end-systole is the optimal target.

Approximately 1-2% of cardiac catheterizations are complicated by femoral pseudoaneurysm formation. An iatrogenic pseudoaneurysm forms when there is contained leakage of blood from a vessel puncture site. The sac of blood communicates with the lumen and continuous flow within the pseudoaneurysm prevents clot formation. Pseudoaneurysms pose a significant risk of rupture with potentially catastrophic consequences if they do. Risk factors for pseudoaneurysm formation include:

Patient related

Anticoagulation

Haemodialysis

Calcified arteries

Obesity

Procedural

Low puncture sites (SFA or profunda femoris)

Suboptimal post-procedure pressure

Some aneurysms do spontaneously thrombose. Ultrasound follow up is not completely unreasonable as a management technique where further intervention is relatively or absolutely contra-indicated, and with appropriate patient counselling regarding risks.

Small pseudoaneurysms (<2cm diameter) can usually be managed non-invasively with manual compression. The goal of manual compression is to occlude the neck of the pseudoaneurysm. This causes stasis within the sac and facilitates clotting. USS is a useful adjunct to compression.

Larger pseudoaneurysms are often amenable to occlusion via ultrasound guided thrombin injection. The average size for pseudoaneurysms amenable to thrombin injection is around 3cm diameter. Larger pseudoaneuryms can be managed with thrombin but it is only safe to perform this if manual compression during the injection is able to satisfactorily occlude the neck of the aneurysm to prevent thrombin embolising distally. Thrombin injection can be used even for patients undergoing anticoagulation with heparin or warfarin and even for higher pseudoaneurysms of the groin region, above the inguinal ligament.

For pseudoaneurysms not amenable to either of these two management strategies surgical ligation would be the next option. Endovascular stenting is not usually performed for femoral pseudoaneurysms owing to the risk of kink formation within the stent on hip flexion. Endovascular coiling is also unsuitable for femoral pseudoaneurysms as the femoral artery is an inexpendable vessel; coiling it would risk leg ischaemia.

prompt: Which of the following is LEAST associated with truncus arteriosus?
explanation: Truncus is classically associated with DiGeorge syndrome (Chromosome 22 abnormality characterised by elongated face and cleft palate, also associated with tetralogy of Fallot). Truncus is also associated with the rarer CHARGE syndrome (Coloboma, congenital Heart disease, choanal atresia, retardation, genital hypoplasia, ear abnormalities). It is also strongly associated with a ventricular septal defect, right sided / interrupted arch. Atrial septal defects can occur in association but are far less common than VSDs.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to A&E with acute left-sided weakness. As part of her initial investigations, she has a CXR which shows a few soft tissue density masses in the left lung. Her only past medical history is of recurrent epistaxis.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In the real world there are many other explanations which could explain this scenario however of the five provided the answer must be something which connects the presence of a lung mass to an acute infarction. Usually the lungs are an excellent filter for micro-emboli however in the presence of a pulmonary AVM (seen as a mass on CXR) these can enter the systemic circulation leading to a CVA. Discounting the epistaxis, breast cancer metastasis would not be an unreasonable differential diagnosis, with the left sided weakness consequent on a cerebral metastasis; certainly breast cancer itself is far more common than Rendu-Osler-Weber syndrome.

Rendu-Osler-Weber syndrome (also known as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia)

There are three separate vascular manifestations of this syndrome; telangiectasias, AVMs and aneurysms. The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and the vast majority of patients will have a positive family history. Hepatic and pulmonary AVMs are a known association and of patients with a pulmonary AVM or AVMs, the prevalence of Rendu-Osler-Weber syndrome is also reasonably high. Pulmonary AVMs have their own spectrum of complications including:

Paradoxical emboli – TIAs and CVAs

Septic emboli – cerebral abscess

Hypoxia due to shunting

High output cardiac failure

In an exam question setting patients are often described as having epistaxis due to nasal telangiectasia, indeed most patients do suffer from frequent episodes. Cutaneous telangiectasias are also common, particularly affecting the lips as well as the oral mucosa and usually by the age of 40. Older patients in their 50s or 60s may experience GI bleeding secondary to angiodysplasia.

explanation:
The femoral artery is the main arterial supply to the lower limb. It is a continuation of the external iliac artery and commences posterior to the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point (halfway between the anterior superior iliac spin and the symphysis pubis).

It emerges from under the inguinal ligament with the femoral vein medial to it and, both within the femoral sheath. The femoral nerve lies lateral to it and outside the femoral sheath. It lies on the tendon of psoas major and is separated from pectineus and adductor longus by the femoral vein, which comes to lie progressively more posterior to the artery within the femoral triangle.

It ends as it passes through the adductor hiatus (Hunter’s canal) in adductor magnus to become the popliteal artery.

The main branch of the femoral artery is the profunda femoris. This is given off posterolaterally just below the femoral sheath 3.5 cm below the inguinal ligament.

The course of the femoral artery (from Gray’s anatomy)

prompt: Which of the following should NOT be used to diagnose a benign pleural lesion over a malignant one?
explanation:
There is a role for PET/CT in lung cancer management however some limitations must be recognised. Currently PET/CT is best used for the N and M staging of the TNM system as a variety of different pathologies can cause both false negatives and false positives for the T staging. Despite this PET/CT does still boast a reasonably high sensitivity and specificity but current teaching suggests that it should not be used in the initial diagnostic process for a lung/pleural cancer, only for staging of a proven malignancy.

Differentiating between benign and malignant lesions is not always straightforward; there is much overlap. There are some features which can strongly indicate in either direction.

Nodular pleural thickening, involvement of the mediastinal pleura and circumferential involvement of the pleura all point heavily towards a malignant diagnosis. The presence of a stalk strongly suggests a benign lesion. Similarly pleural thickening of greater than 8x5x0.3cm is purported to suggest benign pleural plaque disease rather than malignancy.

The features which distinguish benign from malignant should not be confused with those useful in establishing if a lesion is pleural or pulmonary in origin.
