prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)

LAM can go misdiagnosed for many years as emphysema. It occurs exclusively in non-smoking women of childbearing age and quite often a history of spontaneous pneumothorax is given. Radiologically there are numerous small cystic spaces surrounded by normal lung. A chylous pleural effusion (negative Hounsfield units) is reasonably specific. The main differential diagnosis would be histiocytosis which tends to be associated with smoking, classically spares the costophrenic angles and gives small nodules but both can present with spontaneous pneumothorax and give small cysts. The lung volumes in LAM will remain normal whereas they can be increased in Histiocytosis (surprisingly for a fibrotic lung disease).

Histiocytosis (Langerhans cell histiocytosis - LCH)

There are three separate forms of this disease:

Eosinophilic granuloma (70%) – a limited version confined to the skeleton in children or young adults. Clinically presents as fever, raised WCC and ESR with painful bony lesions. In the skull these have a typical ‘beveled edge’ or ‘hole within a hole’ appearance or can be seen as a ‘button sequestrum’. In the spine it is one of the main causes of vertebra plana.

Hand-Schüller-Christian Disease (20%) – classically a triad of destructive bony lesions, diabetes insipidus and exophthalmos. In a quarter of these patients the lungs are involved with cyst formation and spontaneous pneumothoraces possible. Nodule formation, fibrosis and honeycombing are also seen.

Letterer-Siwe Disease (10%) – a fulminant multi-organ variant affecting very young infants

There is a strong association with smoking for patients who develop pulmonary features of LCH. Heavy smoking causes an accumulation of Langerhans cells and hence, as with other inspiration-related lung diseases, there is a predilection for the upper zones. The Langerhans cells can collect with other cells and become small granulomas seen as small lung nodules. Despite being a type of fibrotic lung disease the lung volumes can be increased. Small lung cysts form and there is a risk of spontaneous pneumothorax. There is usually sparing of the costophrenic angles which can be a key finding..

Emphysema

Many cystic lung diseases are often misdiagnosed initially as emphysema, largely due to the population prevalence of emphysema.

True lung cysts however have a perceptible wall whereas emphysematous spaces within lung tissue does not.

Centrilobular emphysema – Caused by smoking. enlargement of the respiratory bronchiole, destruction of the alveolar septa, surrounded by normal lung, distal alveoli are spared. Affects the apical segments of each lobe due to higher ventilation perfusion ratios.

Panacinar emphysema – Caused by alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency. Affects the whole lung with greater severity seen at the bases where there is greater blood flow. Uniform lung destruction.

Paraseptal emphysema – characteristically subpleural. Associated with bullous formation and spontaneous pneumothorax.

Respiratory Bronchiolitis Interstitial Lung disease (RBILD)

This condition is heavily associated with smoking and can be seen as centrilobular nodules with ground glass opacification. Appearances are often very similar to desquamative interstitial pneumonia. Patients can be relatively young.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) also known as either Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) or cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis (CFA)

This is classically a disease of previously fit middle aged men with a reasonably long (>6month) history of shortness of breath and cough. Volume loss is prevalent and there is a classical apico-basilar gradient meaning that the lower zones are much more affected than the upper zones. Honeycombing is classical, particularly subpleural honeycombing. When secondary to a condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or a drug it is known as usual interstitial pneumonia. Overall the prognosis for this condition is extremely poor; worse than that for many common cancers.

Buerger disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)

This disease is strongly linked to smoking and manifests as a vasculitis of the smaller arteries. Arterial occlusion with the formation of corkscrew-shaped collaterals occurs initially in the small arteries of the hands and feet but becoming more proximal as the disease progresses. Of note the larger proximal and central arteries lack the calcification which would otherwise be seen with disease of this extent when caused by atherosclerosis. Patients tend to be younger than those afflicted by atherosclerotic arterial problems.

This arises due to an anomalous insertion of the medial head of gastrocnemius which compresses the popliteal artery leading to symptoms of claudication, particularly on exertion, in an otherwise fit individual. Of note, management is surgical; surgical release has far better outcomes than endovascular stenting.

Cystic adventitial degeneration

On MRI scanning, mucous cysts can be seen in the wall of the popliteal artery. These, like most cysts, show high T2 signal and the T1 signal can be variable depending on the quantity of mucin present. This disease has a strong male preponderance and particularly affects the popliteal artery. On MRI the signal can be variable on T1 depending on the protein content of the cyst but returns a high signal on T2.

stem: A 35-year-old man with a 10 pack year history of smoking undergoes a CT scan of his chest which shows multiple ill defined nodules, honeycombing and interstitial markings.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Histiocytosis (also known as Langerhans cell histiocytosis - LCH)

There are three separate forms of this disease:

Eosinophilic granuloma (70%) – a limited version confined to the skeleton in children or young adults. Clinically presents as fever, raised WCC and ESR with painful bony lesions. In the skull these have a typical ‘beveled edge’ or ‘hole within a hole’ appearance or can be seen as a ‘button sequestrum’. In the spine it is one of the main causes of vertebra plana.

Hand-Schüller-Christian Disease (20%) – classically a triad of destructive bony lesions, diabetes insipidus and exophthalmos. In a quarter of these patients the lungs are involved with cyst formation and spontaneous pneumothoraces possible. Nodule formation, fibrosis and honeycombing is also seen.

Letterer-Siwe Disease (10%) – a fulminant multi-organ variant affecting very young infants

There is a strong association with smoking for patients who develop pulmonary features of LCH. Heavy smoking causes an accumulation of Langerhans cells and hence, as with other inspiration-related lung diseases, there is a predilection for the upper zones. The Langerhans cells can collect with other cells and become small granulomas seen as small lung nodules. Despite being a type of fibrotic lung disease the lung volumes can be increased. Small lung cysts form and there is a risk of spontaneous pneumothorax. There is usually sparing of the costophrenic angles which can be a key finding.

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)

LAM can go misdiagnosed for many years as emphysema. It occurs exclusively in non-smoking women of childbearing age, unlike this patient, and quite often a history of spontaneous pneumothorax is given. Radiologically there are numerous small cystic spaces surrounded by normal lung. A chylous pleural effusion (negative Hounsfield units) is reasonably specific. The main differential diagnosis would be histiocytosis which tends to be associated with smoking, classically spares the costophrenic angles and gives small nodules but both can present with spontaneous pneumothorax and give small cysts. The lung volumes in LAM will remain normal whereas they can be increased in Histiocytosis (surprisingly for a fibrotic lung disease).

Sarcoidosis

‘The great mimic’. In the real world sarcoidosis can appear as almost anything, almost anywhere. Despite this, there are usual ways for sarcoidosis to appear and these are more likely to be tested in exams. The patient in this question could well have sarcoidosis based on the imaging features described however there is no overt link with smoking and therefore LCH is a better answer. The classic patient for pulmonary sarcoidosis is young, female and black with hypercalcaemia. Raised ACE (Angiotensin-converting enzyme) levels should make you think of sarcoidosis, as should a positive Kveim-Siltzbach test (an intracutaneous injection of a suspension of human sarcoid spleen or lymph nodes). Nine out of ten patients with sarcoidosis will have some of thoracic manifestation. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is typical. There are many features considered classical for sarcoidosis:

The ‘1, 2, 3’ sign is present in at least three quarters of patients. It is also called the Garland triad or the pawnbroker's sign and refers to a specific pattern of lymph node enlargement involving both hilar nodes as well as the right paratracheal nodes.

Egg-shell calcification of lymph nodes - this is not exclusive to sarcoidosis but is seen in increasing numbers of patients as the disease duration increases

Traction bronchiectasis.

Upper lobe predominance.

Nodules - these are usually in a perilymphatic distribution but are also found elsewhere. Cavitation can occur but is not typical.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HSP) aka extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA)

This condition is caused by a granulomatous reaction to an inhaled allergen. Consequently it is the upper zones which are most affected. A detailed history should reveal the source of an antigen e.g. malt farmer, bird fancier, proximity to air conditioners etc. On CT EAA appears as widespread patchy ground glass opacification, mosaic in nature with nodules in a centrilobular distribution. Fibrosis and consequential volume loss occurs over months-years of allergen exposure. Involvement of the pleura (including pleural effusions) is very rare which can separate this condition from many others.

Caplan syndrome

This is the name given to the combination of pneumoconiosis and rheumatoid arthritis. It is classically described in coal workers. On CT there are rheumatoid lung nodules in the peripheries and upper zones of the lung as well as features of pneumoconiosis. Pleural effusions are often described as being associated with Caplan syndrome; they may or may not be present.

The consultant radiologist recommends performing a retrospective cardiac gated study through the heart.
prompt: Which of the following is a benefit of a retrospective study over prospective gated study?
explanation:
Retrospective-gated scanning is helical in nature, not acquired in axial blocks. It gives a higher dose to the patient, as the patient is exposed to radiation throughout the entire cardiac cycle, not just one aspect. This allows matching of images to the cardiac cycle and therefore functional information of both valve and left ventricle can be obtained. The resolution and volume of contrast administered does not change between the two techniques.

options: Chemo, radiotherapy and possible curative resection
explanation:
In an ideal world every trainee radiologist would have all the intricacies of staging for all tumour types committed to memory. A qualified subspecialist radiologist could reasonably be expected to be extremely familiar with the staging for cancers within their remit but for the majority of trainees it is simply not practical to memorise each and every staging scheme. As an overall strategy, the most important stages to understand are those which change the management for patients. The patient in this scenario is stage IIIa and thus potentially curable with an aggressive management plan. At Stage IIIb the management changes significantly because stage IIIb and stage IV patients are unresectable. Other facts relating to lung cancer (TNM staging) that are useful to know are those regarding satellite nodules:

Same lobe = T3

Different lobe = T4

Contralateral lung = M1

Post-operative radiotherapy should be offered to the following patient groups:

Patients with N2 level nodes

Patients with positive resection margins

These patients should be WHO performance status 0 or 1 and should also have ‘satisfactory’ pre-operative lung function tests

Post-operative chemotherapy should be offered to:

T1-3

N1-2

(Stage II/III)

For lung cancer some of the important staging features are as follows:

T1 tumours are <3cm

N1 = ipsilateral hilar nodes

T2 tumours are between 3 and 5cm, or involves main bronchus.

N2 = ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal nodes

T3 tumours are any size with extension to:

Chest wall

Pleura or parietal pericardium

Satellite nodules within the same lobe

N3 = contralateral hilar, mediastinal or supraclavicular nodes

M1a = single extrathoracic metastasis, bilateral lesions, malignant pleural effusions.

M1b = multiple extrathoracic metastasis

T4 tumours affect diaphragm, mediastinal organs, carina, vertebral body or satellite nodule in different lobe of same lung.

T1 and T2 both have further subdivisions.

Unresectable tumours are T4, N3 or M1.

Beyond TNM staging patients with similar prognostic outcomes are given further stages. Simple observation of these groupings reveals the following:

Stage I patients MUST be N0

Stage III patients MUST have a sum ≥ 3 (ie T2N2M0, or T1N2M0). [NB some patients with Stage II will also have a sum of 3 (for example T2N1M0) however ALL stage III patients have a sum ≥ 3.]

Stage IIIb patients are unresectable → stage IIIb is denoted either by N3 status or T4N2.

The management of the less common small cell lung cancer is slightly different; the tumours are usually much more aggressive, with earlier metastasis and poorer long term survival statistics. The primary lesion may not be seen separately to the resultant associated nodal mas.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a possible contra-indication to Adenosine stress MRI?
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a contraindication.

Adenosine stress MRI has overtaken dobutamine stress MRI in terms of sensitivity and specificity for investigating the presence of ischaemia or infarction. Adenosine causes coronary vasodilation. If there is a haemodynamically significant stenosis to a coronary vessel, the vessels distal to the stenosis are already maximally dilated to maximise flow and thus the application of adenosine makes no difference to the vessel calibre or the resultant perfusion. Furthermore, the vasodilatation to the remaining unoccluded vessels can 'steal' blood from the stenosed territory and this is seen as hypoperfusion to the affected territory. Dipyridamole (antiplatelet), blocks uptake of adenosine and so patients taking this are also poor candidates for this test, however dipyridimole itself can also induce vasodilatation so may be used as an agent in its own right instead of adenosine.

Contraindications to adenosine include:

Second or third degree heart block

Bronchospasm

Hypotension <90mmHg systolic

Myocardial infarction within 48hrs

Uncontrolled arrhythmia

Severe/critical aortic stenosis

The half-life of adenosine is exceptionally short, around 10 seconds, thus any side effects experienced during the scan resolve very quickly. It also means that during the scan, in order to maintain the effect, the adenosine must be given as an infusion.

Dobutamine stress MRI has been shown to be more sensitive and specific for cardiac disease than a dobutamine stress echocardiogram. It is a sympathomimetic so works by inducing the heart to beat both faster and stronger. By increasing the stress on the whole heart, hitherto compensated areas are unmasked. The drug is given at increasing doses ever 3 minutes until any of:

The heart rate has increased to the target rate of (85% x (200-age))

New wall motion abnormality is seen

Blood pressure rises above 240/220mmHg

Systolic blood pressure falls by 40mmHg

The patient develops persistent arrhythmias

The patient becomes too symptomatic to continue the scan

Aside from the usual contra-indications to performing the MRI in the first place, specific contra-indications to performing a dobutamine stress MRI include:

Hypertension >220/120mmHg

Unstable angina

Aortic stenosis (severe)

Uncontrolled atrial fibrillation

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

prompt: What is the most likely description of the nodules that have been seen as part of this condition?
explanation:
This question is challenging because when describing the CT findings in lymphangitis carcinomatosis it is usually the interstitial and fissural thickening which are of greatest significance. However, nodules can and do occur and when they do they are most commonly found in the subpleural location.

----------------

Lung nodules seen on CT take one of three different patterns:

Perilymphatic nodules

Peribronchiolar, perivascular, subpleural and close to the fissures

Lymphangitis carcinomatosis, sarcoidosis, pneumoconioses

Centrilobular nodules

Found in the centre of the secondary pulmonary lobule, with subpleural sparing

Infections, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, vasculitis

Random

Miliary disease, metastatic disease, langerhans cell histiocytosis

Subpleural nodules are associated with the secondary pulmonary lobule and nodules here represent a perilymphatic distribution such as would be expected with lymphangitis carcinomatosis. They can also be seen in usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) or idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

Please note that the question asks which is INCORRECTLY matched.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Amyloid cardiomyopathy

Amyloidosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning there is global enhancement of the endocardium, and on echocardiogram the myocardium takes on a characteristic granular and speckled appearance. In an exam question setting a history of multiple myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease or similar may be given to suggest secondary amyloidosis.

Sarcoidosis cardiomyopathy

Involvement of the myocardium is relatively rare in sarcoidosis. Inflammation causes myocardial scarring of the interventricular septum and left ventricle most commonly. This shows as epicardial or midwall delayed hyperenhancement on MRI. The patient in this question is certainly of an appropriate demographic for sarcoidosis. The main differential diagnoses would be myocarditis or Chagas disease based on imaging findings alone.

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy

The blood supply to the heart muscle itself is of interest here. The endocardium derives its blood directly from the chambers whereas the layer referred to as the subendocardium receives blood from the terminal branches of the coronary vessels. By the time they reach the subendocardium these blood vessels are small enough that ventricular contraction causes a degree of compression. The end result is that the subendocardium is particularly vulnerable to ischaemia, a fact which manifests in the delayed hyperenhancement patterns seen on MRI; ischaemic cardiomyopathy is seen as subendocardial delayed hyperenhancement or in more extreme cases transmural hyperenhancement. The pattern of hyperenhancement is also territorial with ischaemic cardiomyopathy, depending on which vessel(s) has been affected.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

HCM can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion; there are a number of specific different gene mutations which have been identified to cause cardiac myocardial hypertrophy. The most common category is asymmetrical hypertrophy, accounting for around two thirds of cases. Here the interventricular septum is markedly enlarged. The remaining third of cases display symmetrical/concentric hypertrophy or apical hypertrophy. Patients are younger than most of those with ischaemic cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning midwall hyperenhancement at the junction between the right and left ventricles is typical.

Alcoholic cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy occurs in patients with a history of alcohol abuse. There is dilation of both ventricles alongside thinning of the myocardium which appears hypokinetic on dynamic studies. Myocardial fibrosis occurs and because this typically affects the mid-myocardium it can be differentiated from ischaemic cardiomyopathy which is often transmural and confined to vascular territories. The different areas show delayed enhancement on MRI scans.

explanation:
The brachial artery is the continuation of the axillary artery beginning at the lower margin of teres major. It initially lies medial to the humerus and then spirals around it to lie anterior to it. It is superficial throughout its course and is accompanied by venae commitantes. It is the main source of blood to the arm.

Immediately distal to teres major it gives rise to the profunda brachii (the deep artery of the arm). The profunda brachii passes posteriorly between the long and medial head of triceps with the radial nerve into the spiral groove of the humerus before breaking up into its terminal branches.

The brachial artery gives of the superior ulnar collateral artery just below the level of the mid arm. It then gives off the inferior ulnar collateral artery about 5 cm above the elbow.

It is closely related to the median nerve throughout its course. Initially the median nerve lies immediately lateral to the brachial artery but it crosses over to the medial side at the mid arm. It is also crossed by the bicipital aponeurosis in the cubital fossa.

The pulse of the brachial artery is palpable on the anterior aspect of the elbow, medial to the biceps tendon. It is at this site that blood pressure is often measured using a stethoscope and sphygmomanometer.

The brachial artery ends in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius by bifurcating into its terminal branches, the radial and ulnar arteries.

Rheumatic heart disease is associated with both aortic stenosis and mitral stenosis simultaneously. It is caused by previous Group A-Beta haemolytic strep.

Williams Syndrome

Williams syndrome is chromosomal disease and a recognised cause of supravalvular aortic and pulmonary stenosis.

Turner’s syndrome

Turner’s is another genetic disease (45XO). Is associated with bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation.

Ebstein anomaly

Most cases are sporadic, but it is associated with maternal lithium use. Classically these patients have a ‘box-shaped’ heart on chest radiograph. They have a prolapsing tricuspid valve with atrialization of the right ventricle.

Alagille syndrome

This is a genetic multisystem disease. With regards to cardiac issues, it causes coarctation of the aorta and peripheral pulmonary stenosis.

options: It is continuous with the central tendon of the diaphragm
It is continuous with the heart
It is divided into two layers
It is thinner than the serous pericardium
explanation:
The pericardium is a double-walled sac containing the heart and the roots of the great vessels. It is made up of two layers, the external fibrous pericardium, and the internal serous pericardium.

The fibrous pericardium is thicker and tougher than the serous pericardium and is continuous with the central tendon of the diaphragm. It is made up of dense and loose connective tissue, which protects the heart, anchoring it to the surrounding walls, and preventing it from overfilling with blood.

The serous pericardium is thinner than the fibrous pericardium and is itself divided into two layers:

The parietal pericardium, which is the outer layer and is fused to and inseparable from the fibrous pericardium.

The visceral pericardium, which is the inner layer and forms the outer layer of the heart.

The visceral pericardium extends to the beginning of the great vessels and becomes one with the parietal pericardium where the aorta and pulmonary trunk leave the heart and where the superior and inferior vena cava, and the pulmonary veins enter the heart. Where the visceral layer comes into contact with the heart it is referred to as the epicardium.

The pericardial cavity, which contains the lubricating pericardial fluid, is found between the parietal and visceral pericardium.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is responsible for the innervation of the pericardium. Inflammation of the pericardium, for example in pericarditis, can therefore cause referred pain to other somatic regions served by spinal nerves C3-C5. This is the reason why patients with pericarditis sometimes experience shoulder tip pain.

The fibrous pericardium is tough and inextensible, which helps with protection of the heart but can also cause problems when a pericardial effusion develops within the pericardial cavity. The rigid nature of this layer means that as an effusion develops and pressure increases within the pericardial cavity, the cardiac chambers become compressed and cardiac output is compromised.

The pericardial cavity, which contains the lubricating pericardial fluid, is found between the parietal and visceral pericardium. The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is responsible for the innervation of the pericardium. Inflammation of the pericardium, for example in pericarditis, can therefore cause referred pain to other somatic regions served by spinal nerves C3-C5. This is the reason why patients with pericarditis sometimes experience shoulder tip pain. The fibrous pericardium is tough and inextensible, which helps with protection of the heart but can also cause problems when a pericardial effusion develops within the pericardial cavity. The rigid nature of this layer means that as an effusion develops and pressure increases within the pericardial cavity, the cardiac chambers become compressed and cardiac output is compromised. prompt: The right gonadal vein drains into the inferior vena cava at which vertebral level? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The inferior vena cava carries deoxygenated blood from all of the structures lying below the diaphragm into the right atrium of the heart. It arises as the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the L5 vertebral level.

It ascends upwards in the retroperitoneal space, to the right of the lumbar vertebral bodies and to the right of the aorta. It pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level to enter the thorax. It then almost immediately enters the pericardium before draining into the right atrium.

The inferior vena cava receives tributaries from:

Common iliac veins (origin at L5) – drain lower limbs and gluteal regions

Lumbar veins (between L1 and L5) – drain the posterior abdominal wall

Right gonadal vein (L2) – drain the right testis/ovary

Renal veins (L1) – drain the kidneys, left adrenal gland, left testis/ovary

Right adrenal vein (L1) – drains the right adrenal gland

Right, middle and left hepatic veins (T8) – drain the liver

Right and left inferior phrenic veins (T8) – drain the diaphragm

The ribs are narrow, curved, flat bones that form most of the thoracic cage.

The true ribs are the first seven ribs (sometimes eight). They are called the true ribs because they attach the vertebrae to the sternum through their costal cartilages.

The false ribs are the 8th to the 10th ribs (the vertebrochondral ribs). They are called the false ribs because their cartilages are joined to the cartilage of the rib just superior to them.

The floating ribs are the 11th and 12th ribs. They are called the false ribs because their cartilages end in the posterior abdominal musculature.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Buerger disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)

This disease is strongly linked to smoking and manifests as a vasculitis of the smaller arteries. Arterial occlusion with the formation of corkscrew-shaped collaterals occurs initially in the small arteries of the hands and feet but becoming more proximal as the disease progresses. Of note the larger proximal and central arteries lack the calcification which would otherwise be seen with disease of this extent when caused by atherosclerosis. Patients tend to be younger than those afflicted by atherosclerotic arterial problems.

Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (PAES)

This arises due to an anomalous insertion of the medial head of gastrocnemius which compresses the popliteal artery leading to symptoms of claudication, particularly on exertion, in an otherwise fit individual. Of note, management is surgical; surgical release has far better outcomes than endovascular stenting.

Cystic adventitial degeneration

On MRI scanning, mucous cysts can be seen in the wall of the popliteal artery. These, like most cysts, show high T2 signal and the T1 signal can be variable depending on the quantity of mucin present. This disease has a strong male preponderance and particularly affects the popliteal artery. On MRI the signal can be variable on T1 depending on the protein content of the cyst but returns a high signal on T2.

Atherosclerosis

This is very common and particularly prevalent among older patients, particularly smokers and particularly those with high cholesterol levels. On imaging the vessel walls show calcification and plaque formation occurs.

The cardiac muscle nulls easily on post contrast sequences in cardiac amyloidosis
explanation:
Cardiac MRI - a brief overview

On post contrast sequences in cardiac amyloidosis the signal from the cardiac muscle is nulled however owing to the presernce of scar tissue throughout the muscle it can be challenging to identiy an appropriate area of muscle to use as a guide to null the signal. This is a feature very specific to cardiac amyloidosis.

A small amount of physics for imaging of patients with cardiac amyloidosis

Amyloid deposition leads to fibrosis and, as a general rule, fibrotic processes contain little water. On MRI scans therefore, most fibrotic entities return little signal on any sequence. Additionally, in many patients with amyloid cardiomyopathy, gadolinium washes out of the myocardium far faster than normally occurs. Both these features combine to the extent that the blood within the heart becomes very dark (due to higher than usual concentrations of gadolinium washed out from the myocardium) but at the same time the signal from the myocardium is very low due to the presence of fibrosis. Nulling the signal from the myocardium (to try to better visualise the affected areas of myocardium) therefore becomes difficult since the null point for both the blood pool and the myocardium is almost the same.

SSFP or FSE - used to look for gross abnormalities in the whole chest, and to plan further cardiac views. Cine-SSFP used to look at ventricle and valve function, volume, mass and ejection fraction. Early post contrast T1 FSE sequences are useful to look for early hyperenhancement which is a sign of inflammation such as myocarditis or pericarditis. First-pass perfusion (can be FSE or GRE) sequences are not essential but can be useful to examine for peri-infarction ischaemia. The ischaemic areas are seen as dark against the enhancement of normal myocardium.

GRE - used to examine delayed enhancement. Images taken around 15 minutes (10-20mins) after gadolinium is injected. Normal myocardium undergoes a rapid wash-in and wash-out of contrast, but abnormal myocardium has a slower wash-in and wash-out so is still enhancing at this time. Myocardial infarction can be seen as an area of delayed hyperenhancement, classically in a vascular territorial distribution and also classically involving the subendocardium (which is usually spared in non-ischaemic pathology). Delayed hyperenhancement in a pattern typical for ischaemia is highly sensitive for both chronic and acute myocardial infarction.

explanation:
Both lung cancer and round atelectasis show enhancement post contrast.

A lack of association with pleural plaques would make this lesion even more suspicious for lung cancer than if they were present when the possibility of round atelectasis is more likely. Having said that, even in the presence of pleural plaques, of course a lung cancer would still need to be excluded.

Round atelectasis

Round atelectasis occurs most commonly as part of the spectrum of asbestos related findings but does have other lesser aetiologies. It is also referred to as ‘infolded lung’ which better describes the appearances seen on CT. On CT there is a rounded mass-like region adjacent to the pleural surface. A comet tail sign is seen coming from the mass where the bronchovascular structures supplying the affected part of the lung are pulled into the centre of it thus there is a linear opacity curving outwards from the mass and pointing towards the hilum. The pleura adjacent to the mass is often thickened and if the mass is sufficiently large, features of volume loss can be seen in the ipsilateral hemithorax. Owing to the association with asbestos the patient may well show other features of exposure such as pleural plaque disease.

Pleural plaques

When calcified pleural plaques are seen bilaterally it is virtually pathognomonic of prior asbestos exposure. Of all asbestos related pleural plaques around 85% are calcified. Involvement of the mediastinum should raise the possibility of mesothelioma but involvement of the costophrenic angles should raise the possibility of an alternative diagnosis as these are usually spared in asbestos related plaque disease. Unilateral pleural plaques can be caused by any previous insult such as surgery or an empyema although the most common cause is still asbestos related lung disease.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Aspergillosis

How the fungus aspergillus affects a patient depends on their underlying immune status.

Severely immunocompromised patients → Invasive aspergillosis

Mildly immunocompromised patients → semi-invasive aspergillosis

Normal patients → non-invasive aspergillosis (such as colonization of a pre-existing cyst or cavity)

Hypersensitive patients (Cystic fibrosis or asthmatics) → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)

ABPA

ABPA causes a ‘migratory pneumonitis’, typically affecting the upper lobes. Parenchymal changes are fleeting; appearing in one area of the lung one week and a different area the next. The ‘finger in glove’ sign can often be seen, where mucus plugging of a bronchus allows the distal airway to fill with secretions giving rise to a ‘V’ or Y’ shaped shadow on a CXR or CT. This is known as a finger in glove sign owing to its appearance. Central bronchiectasis is a prominent feature and is can be given in an exam question setting as ‘ring shadows’ on a CXR. The peripheral bronchi are classically spared. Cavity formation is seen in the later stages of the disease although aspergillomas are not typical (these occur in patients with a normal immune system). The typical patient in an exam question setting will be young, with a history of either asthma or cystic fibrosis or ‘chronic lung disease’, symptoms of malaise, headache and intermittent chest pains, and an eosinophilia on their full blood count.

The differential diagnosis for the gloved finger sign includes:

ABPA

Cystic fibrosis

Bronchogenic carcinoma

Congenital lobar overinflation

Bronchial atresia

Invasive aspergillosis

Invasive aspergillosis is one of the ways in which the fungus aspergillus can affect the lungs. It occurs only in patients with a severely compromised immune system such as those with AIDs, on high dose steroids or (like the patient in the question) neutropenic. There is endobronchial fungal growth with vascular invasion leading to microthrombosis and microinfarction. This is seen initially as a characteristic halo sign which over the ensuing two weeks undergoes necrosis and cavitation developing as it does so, an air crescent sign. Although this is a different process to the creation of a Monod sign (air crescent at the superior aspect of an aspergilloma) they can seem similar.

The halo sign

The halo sign is used to describe the appearance of a nodule surrounded by a ‘halo’ of ground glass opacification. It occurs when there is alveolar haemorrhage and is considered to be a classical finding in invasive aspergillosis. It is also seen in a number of other conditions:

Haemorrhagic metastases – Malignant melanoma, choriocarcinoma, osteosarcoma, angiosarcoma

Bronchioalveolar carcinoma (now called minimally invasive adenocarcinoma)

Other fungal infections

Mycobacterial infections (TB and atypicals)

Wegener granulomatosis

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

options: It begins at the lower border of teres major
It initially lies lateral to the humerus
It is a continuation of the subclavian artery
It is crossed from medial to lateral by the median nerve at the mid arm
Its pulse is palpable lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow
explanation:
The brachial artery is the continuation of the axillary artery beginning at the lower margin of teres major. It initially lies medial to the humerus and then spirals around it to lie anterior to it. It is superficial throughout its course and is accompanied by venae commitantes. It is the main source of blood to the arm.

Immediately distal to teres major it gives rise to the profunda brachii (the deep artery of the arm). The profunda brachii passes posteriorly between the long and medial head of triceps with the radial nerve into the spiral groove of the humerus before breaking up into its terminal branches.

The brachial artery gives of the superior ulnar collateral artery just below the level of the mid arm. It then gives off the inferior ulnar collateral artery about 5 cm above the elbow.

It is closely related to the median nerve throughout its course. Initially the median nerve lies immediately lateral to the brachial artery but it crosses over to the medial side at the mid arm. It is also crossed by the bicipital aponeurosis in the cubital fossa.

The pulse of the brachial artery is palpable on the anterior aspect of the elbow, medial to the biceps tendon. It is at this site that blood pressure is often measured using a stethoscope and sphygmomanometer.

The brachial artery ends in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius by bifurcating into its terminal branches, the radial and ulnar arteries.

In an ideal world every trainee radiologist would have all the intricacies of staging for all tumour types committed to memory. A qualified subspecialist radiologist could reasonably be expected to be extremely familiar with the staging for cancers within their remit but for the majority of trainees it is simply not practical to memorise each and every staging scheme. As an overall strategy, the most important stages to understand are those which change the management for patients. At Stage IIIb the management changes significantly because stage IIIb and stage IV patients are unresectable. Other facts relating to lung cancer (TNM staging) that are useful to know are those regarding satellite nodules:

Same lobe = T3

Different lobe = T4

Contralateral lung = M1

For lung cancer some of the important staging features are as follows (TNM 8th edition):

T1 tumours are <3cm

N1 = ipsilateral hilar nodes

T2 tumours are between 3 and 5cm, or involves main bronchus.

N2 = ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal nodes

T3 tumours are any size with extension to:

Chest wall

Pleura or parietal pericardium

Satellite nodules within the same lobe

N3 = contralateral hilar, mediastinal or supraclavicular nodes

M1a = single extrathoracic metastasis, bilateral lesions, malignant pleural effusions.

M1b = multiple extrathoracic metastasis

T4 tumours affect diaphragm, mediastinal organs, carina, vertebral body or satellite nodule in different lobe of same lung.

T1 and T2 both have further subdivisions.

Unresectable tumours are T4, N3 or M1.

Beyond TNM staging patients with similar prognostic outcomes are given further stages. Simple observation of these groupings reveals the following:

Stage I patients MUST be N0

Stage III patients MUST have a sum ≥ 3 (ie T2N2M0, or T1N2M0). [NB some patients with Stage II will also have a sum of 3 (for example T2N1M0) however ALL stage III patients have a sum ≥ 3.]

Stage IIIb patients are unresectable → stage IIIb is denoted either by N3 status or T4N2.

prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the aorta is true?
options: It initially lies anterior to the pulmonary trunk
It runs through a common pericardial sheath with the pulmonary trunk
Its first major branch is the left subclavian artery
The aortic arch passes beneath the left main bronchus
The posterior aortic sinus gives rise to the right coronary artery
explanation:
The aorta receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and delivers it to the body. It can be divided into three parts:

The ascending aorta

The arch of the aorta

The descending aorta

The ascending aorta commences at the opening of the aortic valve in the left ventricle of the heart. It runs through a common pericardial sheath with the pulmonary trunk. The ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk twist around each other, with the aorta initially lying posterior to the pulmonary trunk, before twisting to the right and lying anteriorly to it.

At the root of the ascending aorta, the lumen contains three aortic sinuses. The left aortic sinus contains the origin of the left coronary artery and the right aortic sinus contains the right coronary artery. Together these two arteries supply the heart. The third sinus, which is called the posterior aortic sinus, does not give rise to a coronary artery.

The aortic arch commences at the point of the pericardial reflection on the aorta, which is posterior to the manubriosternal joint at the level of the second costal cartilage. It passes posterior and to the left, over the left main bronchus and ends at the left side of the body of the 4th thoracic vertebra. Its highest level is the mid point of the manubrium sterni and it is at this level that its three main branches arise:

Brachiocephalic artery, which supplies blood to the brain, head, and right side of the thorax

Left common carotid artery, which supplies blood to the left side of the head and neck

Left subclavian artery, which supplies blood to the left side of the thorax

The descending aorta commences at the end of the arch of the aorta, which is at the level of the intervertebral disc between the 4th and 5th thoracic vertebrae. The descending aorta, in turn, becomes then thoracic and abdominal aorta.

The aorta and its three main branches

Histoplasmosis in the context of AIDs does not usually demonstrate a tree-in-bud appearance.

Histoplasmosis

In immunocompetent individuals infection with histoplasmosis is sub-clinical in the vast majority of cases. In immunodeficient patients however it is a different story; it can be fatal. AIDs patients are at risk if their CD4 count is below 150cells/mm3.

Patients present in a non-specific manner with fever, malaise, diarrhoea, and vomiting but around half will have no CXR findings. On CT miliary disease is seen as well as reticulonodular and air space opacities. Like cryptococcal, histoplasma is found in bird excreta.

Tree-in-bud

A tree-in-bud pattern occurs when the lumen of the terminal bronchiole is filled with radiopaque material. Historically the appearance was associated most strongly with tuberculosis however it is more recently recognized as a feature common to many different pathologies. The nature of the material depends on the underlying pathology. For instance:

Pus – mycobacterial infection

Mucus – cystic fibrosis

Cells – breast cancer, stomach cancer (infiltration of the centrilobular artery with tumour cells)

Aspirated substances

Inflammatory infiltrate – autoimmune conditions

Bronchial wall thickening - CMV

Here we are given the term tree-in-bud but this can also be indicated with a visual description of this entity such as ‘small centrilobular nodules connected by branching opacities’ or words to that effect.

AIDs

AIDs defining illnesses pertinent to the thoracic radiology include, among others:

Tuberculosis

CMV pneumonia

Histoplasmosis pneumonia

Kaposi sarcoma

MAC

PCP also known as PJP

Cryptococcal pneumonia

Needless to say not all patients with HIV have AIDs.

explanation:
A pleural effusion is excess fluid that accumulates in the pleural cavity, the fluid filled space that is situated between the parietal and visceral pleura. The pleural cavity usually contains between 5-10 ml of this lubricating fluid. This fluid lubricates the surfaces of the pleurae, allowing them to slide over each other. It also produces a surface tension that pulls the two membranes together and ensures that as the thorax expands, the lungs do also and fill with air. Excess fluid in the pleural cavity impairs breathing by limiting expansion of the lungs.

Percutaneous pleural aspiration is generally carried out for two main indications:

For investigation of pleural effusion

For symptomatic relief of breathlessness caused by pleural effusion

The British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines suggest that pleural aspiration should be reserved for the investigation of unilateral exudative pleural effusions. It should not be carried out if unilateral or bilateral transudative effusion is suspected, unless there are atypical features or failure of response to therapy. It can also be used for the urgent decompression of the pleural space for the relief of respiratory distress caused by pleural effusion.

The procedure is usually carried out with the patient sat upright with a pillow nused to support their arms and head. The patient should not lean forwards too much as it increases the risk of injury to the liver and spleen.

The conventional site for aspiration is posteriorly in the mid-scapular line (approximately 10 cm lateral to the spine), one or two spaces below the upper level of the fluid. The needle should be inserted just above the upper border of the chosen rib to avoid the intercostal nerves and vessels that run immediately below the rib.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Papillary fibroelastoma

These tumours are rare even for cardiac tumours but yet are the most common cardiac tumour to be associated with the valves. Rather counter-intuitively, they do not cause valvular dysfunction. They are usually quite small and, like myxomas, relatively mobile, attached by a stalk, and able to prolapse through a valve but where myxomas usually arise from the interatrial septum, papillary fibroelastomas grow from the valve itself. Histopathologically they are gelatinous tumours resembling sea anemones with multiple papillary projections. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided masses. On MRI they are often low in signal on T2 weighted sequences owing to their fibrous nature.

Atrial thrombus

The usual site for an atrial thrombus would be the left atrial appendage. Thrombi are not seen as mobile masses but as irregular lobulated masses. They can have a laminated appearance and the classical feature is low signal on gradient-echo MRI sequences owing to the presence of haemosiderin (blooming artefact). They do not enhance. Ventricular thrombi can form too, it is usually a sequela of a previous myocardial infarction which has healed leaving a hypomobile portion of the ventricular wall. Adjacent to that part of wall there is relative stasis sufficient to facilitate thrombus formation.

Atrial myxoma

These are the most common benign neoplasms of the heart. Although usually sporadic, they can occur as part of Carney syndrome (atrial myxoma, facial/buccal pigmentation, sertoli tumours of the testis and multiple other findings. Not to be confused with Carney triad - pulmonary hamartomas, gastric leiomyosarcomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas). The finding of a small mass attached to the interatrial septum by a stalk is classical. Their mobility allows some to prolapse through the relevant atrioventricular valve during the cardiac cycle. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for the more common left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided myxomas. Iso or hypointensity on T1w MRI is typical.

Carney Triad

Carney Syndrome

1. Pulmonary harmatoma

Atrial myxoma

2. Gastric leiomyosarcoma (GIST)

Facial/ buccal pigmentation

3. Extra-adrenal paraganglioma

Sertoli tumour of the testis

Pituitary adenoma

Cardiac sarcoma

There are many different types of cardiac sarcoma. Cardiac sarcomas are the most common cause of primary malignant cardiac tumours. Their presentation usually relates either to embolic phenomena such as TIAs or symptoms from invasion such as pericardial effusion. In contrast to myxomas or fibroelastomas, malignant lesions tend to have a broad attachment to the heart wall. Another useful differentiating feature on imaging is the involvement of more than one chamber of the heart.

Cardiac metastases

Metastases are significantly more common than cardiac sarcomas meaning metastases are the most common malignant cardiac tumours. In contrast to myxomas or fibroelastomas, malignant lesions tend to have a broad attachment to the heart wall. Tumours can be from lung or breast cancer, lymphoma, leukaemia and malignant melanoma.

prompt: Which of the following features will help distinguish between a malignant and a benign lesion?
options: The angle made with the chest wall
explanation:
Differentiating between benign and malignant lesions is not always straightforward; there is much overlap. There are some features which can strongly indicate in either direction.

Nodular pleural thickening, involvement of the mediastinal pleura and circumferential involvement of the pleura all point heavily towards a malignant diagnosis. The presence of a stalk strongly suggests a benign lesion. Similarly the pleural thickening of 8x5x0.3cm given in the answer, being less than 1cm thick, suggests benign pleural plaque disease rather than malignancy.

The features which distinguish benign from malignant should not be confused with those useful in establishing if a lesion is pleural or pulmonary in origin.

Pleural/ Extrapleural

Pulmonary

Doesn’t displace extrapleural fat

In general, malignant lesions of the heart have a broad-based attachment to the heart whereas benign pathology has a narrow-based attachment or none at all in the case of a thrombus.

Cardiac metastases

Metastases are significantly more common than cardiac sarcomas meaning metastases are the most common malignant cardiac tumours. In contrast to myxomas or fibroelastomas, malignant lesions tend to have a broad attachment to the heart wall. Tumours can be from lung or breast cancer, lymphoma, leukaemia and malignant melanoma.

Papillary fibroelastoma

These tumours are rare even for cardiac tumours but yet are the most common cardiac tumour to be associated with the valves. Rather counter-intuitively, they do not cause valvular dysfunction. They are usually quite small and, like myxomas, relatively mobile, attached by a stalk, and able to prolapse through a valve but where myxomas usually arise from the interatrial septum, papillary fibroelastomas grow from the valve itself. Histopathologically they are gelatinous tumours resembling sea anemones with multiple papillary projections. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided masses. On MRI they are often low in signal on T2 weighted sequences owing to their fibrous nature.

Atrial thrombus

The usual site for an atrial thrombus would be the left atrial appendage. Thrombi are not seen as mobile masses but as irregular lobulated masses. They can have a laminated appearance and the classical feature is low signal on gradient-echo MRI sequences owing to the presence of haemosiderin (blooming artefact). They do not enhance. Ventricular thrombi can form too, it is usually a sequela of a previous myocardial infarction which has healed leaving a hypomobile portion of the ventricular wall. Adjacent to that part of wall there is relative stasis sufficient to facilitate thrombus formation.

Atrial myxoma

These are the most common benign neoplasms of the heart. Although usually sporadic, they can occur as part of Carney syndrome (atrial myxoma, facial/buccal pigmentation, sertoli tumours of the testis and multiple other findings. Not to be confused with Carney triad - pulmonary chondromas, gastric leiomyosarcomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas). The finding of a small mass attached to the interatrial septum by a stalk is classical. Their mobility allows some to prolapse through the relevant atrioventricular valve during the cardiac cycle. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for the more common left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided myxomas. Iso or hypointensity on T1w MRI is typical.

Carney Syndrome

FDG imaging relies on glucose uptake being increased in tissues of interest which are more metabolically active than non-target tissues. Hence the patient must be fasted such that the FDG given is taken up rapidly enough to produce an image.

FDG is renally excreted. Patients with a poor renal function are at risk of enduring a higher dose than those with a normal renal function. However, assuming the dose is correctly adjusted down there is no reason such patients cannot undergo PET/CT scanning.

Insulin treatment does not preclude imaging, and indeed helps reduce the extracellular glucose concentration thereby improving the quality of scans acquired later. There should be at least a 4-hour gap between the last insulin dose and the FDG tracer dose time.

The literature on fasting varies and different organizations have suggested slightly different fasting windows. The most conservative of these is 6 hours.

Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine must be avoided for at least 12 hours prior to the scan.

Exercise should be avoided for 24, if not 48 hours prior to the scan.

explanation:
The trachea marks the start of the tracheobronchial tree, arising at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, as a continuation of the larynx. This is at the C6 vertebral level.

It travels inferiorly into the superior mediastinum, bifurcating at the level of the sternal angle to form the right and left bronchi. Inside the trachea, at the T5 vertebral level, there is a cartilaginous ridge called the carina of trachea that marks the point of bifurcation. During its descent the trachea is located anterior to the oesophagus and inclines slightly to the right.

Below the cricoid cartilage there are 15 to 20 incomplete C-shaped tracheal rings (tracheal cartilages), which are composed of hyaline cartilage, and serve to reinforce the front and sides of the trachea to protect and maintain the airway. The free ends of these rings are supported by the trachealis muscle.

The trachea and bronchi are lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, interspersed by goblet cells, which produce mucous. The combination of sweeping movements by the cilia and mucous from the goblet cells forms the functional mucociliary escalator, that traps particles and pathogens and moves them up and out of the airways to be swallowed and destroyed.

In contrast to myxomas or fibroelastomas, malignant lesions tend to have a broad attachment to the heart wall. Involvement of more than one chamber of the heart, regardless of which side is involved, is a strong indicator of malignancy. With regards which side of the heart is affected; the most common kind of cardiac sarcoma is an angiosarcoma and these have a predilection for the right side of the heart however they are also found on the left side, and angiosarcomas account for less than 50% of all sarcomas, the remainder of which are more commonly (though not exclusively) found on the left. Cardiac metastases Metastases are significantly more common than cardiac sarcomas meaning metastases are the most common malignant cardiac tumours. In contrast to myxomas or fibroelastomas, malignant lesions tend to have a broad attachment to the heart wall. Tumours can be from lung or breast cancer, lymphoma, leukaemia and malignant melanoma. Papillary fibroelastoma These tumours are rare even for cardiac tumours but yet are the most common cardiac tumour to be associated with the valves. Rather counter-intuitively, they do not cause valvular dysfunction. They are usually quite small and, like myxomas, relatively mobile, attached by a stalk, and able to prolapse through a valve but where myxomas usually arise from the interatrial septum, papillary fibroelastomas grow from the valve itself. Histopathologically they are gelatinous tumours resembling sea anemones with multiple papillary projections. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided masses. On MRI they are often low in signal on T2 weighted sequences owing to their fibrous nature. Atrial thrombus The usual site for an atrial thrombus would be the left atrial appendage. Thrombi are not seen as mobile masses but as irregular lobulated masses. They can have a laminated appearance and the classical feature is low signal on gradient-echo MRI sequences owing to the presence of haemosiderin (blooming artefact). They do not enhance. Ventricular thrombi can form too, it is usually a sequela of a previous myocardial infarction which has healed leaving a hypomobile portion of the ventricular wall. Adjacent to that part of wall there is relative stasis sufficient to facilitate thrombus formation. Atrial myxoma These are the most common benign neoplasms of the heart. Although usually sporadic, they can occur as part of Carney complex (atrial myxoma, facial/buccal pigmentation, sertoli tumours of the testis and multiple other findings. Not to be confused with Carney triad - pulmonary hamartomas, gastric leiomyosarcomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas). The finding of a small mass attached to the interatrial septum by a stalk is classical. Their mobility allows some to prolapse through the relevant atrioventricular valve during the cardiac cycle. They can act as a focus for platelet aggregation leading to systemic emboli for the more common left sided masses or pulmonary emboli for right sided myxomas. Iso or hypointensity on T1w MRI is typical. Carney Triad Carney Complex 1. Pulmonary chondroma Atrial myxoma 2. Gastric leiomyosarcoma (GIST) Facial/ buccal pigmentation 3. prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the serous pericardium is true? Select ONE answer only.
options: It is continuous with the central tendon of the diaphragm
It is divided into three layers
It is the external layer of the pericardium
It is thicker than the fibrous perciardium
explanation:
The pericardium is a double-walled sac containing the heart and the roots of the great vessels. It is made up of two layers, the external fibrous pericardium, and the internal serous pericardium.

The fibrous pericardium is thicker and tougher than the serous pericardium and is continuous with the central tendon of the diaphragm. It is made up of dense and loose connective tissue, which protects the heart, anchoring it to the surrounding walls, and preventing it from overfilling with blood.

The serous pericardium is thinner than the fibrous pericardium and is itself divided into two layers:

The parietal pericardium, which is the outer layer and is fused to and inseparable from the fibrous pericardium.

The visceral pericardium, which is the inner layer and forms the outer layer of the heart.

The visceral pericardium extends to the beginning of the great vessels and becomes one with the parietal pericardium where the aorta and pulmonary trunk leave the heart and where the superior and inferior vena cava, and the pulmonary veins enter the heart. Where the visceral layer comes into contact with the heart it is referred to as the epicardium.

The pericardial cavity, which contains the lubricating pericardial fluid, is found between the parietal and visceral pericardium.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is responsible is responsible for the innervation of the pericardium. Inflammation of the pericardium, for example in pericarditis, can therefore cause referred pain to other somatic regions served by spinal nerves C3-C5. This is the reason why patients with pericarditis sometimes experience shoulder tip pain.

The fibrous pericardium is tough and inextensible, which helps with protection of the heart but can also cause problems when a pericardial effusion develops within the pericardial cavity. The rigid nature of this layer means that as an effusion develops and pressure increases within the pericardial cavity, the cardiac chambers become compressed and cardiac output is compromised.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with shortness of breath. He undergoes an echocardiogram and subsequently a cardiac MRI scan which demonstrate bi-atrial dilatation with a normal ventricular size. These investigations also suggest the presence of biventricular thrombus and endocardial fibrosis. Serum eosinophilia is raised.
prompt: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Loeffler endocarditis (eosinophilic cardiomyopathy)

Biventricular ventricular thrombus with endocardial fibrosis is a classical description of this condition. It can cause both a restrictive cardiomyopathy and valvular pathology. Elevation of serum eosinophil levels is another feature.

Loeffler endocarditis is part of a spectrum of idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome and takes its name from the same physician who also defined pulmonary eosinophilia as 'Loeffler syndrome'. Thus a patient with idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome may have both Loeffler endocarditis and Loeffler syndrome, or they can exist in isolation. Technically, Loeffler originally described pulmonary eosinophilia only in cases following parasitic infections however if no such cause is identified then the term 'simple pulmonary eosinophilia' is more correct, although there is overlap in the literature.

Amyloid

This is the most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. There is often diffuse subendocardial delayed gadolinium enhancement; this is a classic feature. Cardiac MRI studies on patients with amyloid cardiomyopathy can often be technically very challenging to perform.

A small amount of physics for imaging of patients with cardiac amyloidosis

Amyloid deposition leads to fibrosis and, as a general rule, fibrotic processes contain little water. On MRI scans therefore, most fibrotic entities return little signal on any sequence. Additionally, in many patients with amyloid cardiomyopathy, gadolinium washes out of the myocardium far faster than normally occurs. Both these features combine to the extent that the blood within the heart becomes very dark (due to higher than usual concentrations of gadolinium washed out from the myocardium) but at the same time the signal from the myocardium is very low due to the presence of fibrosis. Nulling the signal from the myocardium (to try to better visualise the affected areas of myocardium) therefore becomes difficult since the null point for both the blood pool and the myocardium is almost the same.

TB

TB can affect the pericardium and result in constrictive pericarditis. It can also affect the myocardium and give a nodular appearance to the myocardium on T1.

Sarcoidosis

This usually causes nodular midwall late gadolinium enhancement, particularly affecting the base of the septum.

Atrial Fibrillation

This can cause biatrial dilatation, but is not associated with the other features.

stem: You are reviewing the HRCT of a 64-year-old man. He has been experiencing recurrent tachycardia, but this is well controlled on regular medication. The CT shows high attenuation in the liver and bilateral changes in the lower lobes of the lungs.
prompt: What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Amiodarone therapy

Amiodarone is an anti-arrhythmic drug which contains iodine (am-IOD-arone). Consequently, as it accumulates in the liver, it can cause significant increase in density to the liver on a CT scan.

Around 10% of patients taking Amiodarone can develop lung disease from it. These patients are usually older than 60 and have been taking Amiodarone for around 2-6 months. On an HRCT scan ground glass opacities, reticulations and areas of consolidation can be seen. The constellation of lung changes seen represent a kind of non-specific interstitial pneumonitis as well as an organising pneumonia type of pattern (NSIP and COP).

Around half of patients can develop pleural effusions.

prompt: Contraction of the thoracic diaphragm will result in which of the following? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The thoracic diaphragm is a double-domed sheet of skeletal muscle that serves as the primary muscle of respiration. It is located at the inferior-most aspect of the ribcage, acting as the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominal cavity.

The diaphragm is the primary muscle involved in inspiration. When it contracts, it moves inferiorly moving the abdominal viscera and increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity. This in turn decreases the intra-thoracic pressure and causes air to be drawn into the lungs. This also results in a small decrease in the volume of the abdominal cavity and slightly increases the intra-abdominal pressure.

During expiration the diaphragm passively relaxes and returns to its original shape. This restores the volume of the thoracic cavity and increases the intra-thoracic pressure.

Movements of the diaphragm also play an important role in regulating the circulation. The increase in intra-abdominal pressure and decrease in intra-thoracic pressure that occurs with inspiration resulting in an increase in venous return.

stem: A 35-year-old man driving his car at 60mph is involved in a severe road traffic accident and is brought into the Emergency Department. He is too unstable to undergo a CT scan, but a trauma series of radiographs is taken. The chest x-ray has a number of findings which make you suspicious of an aortic transection.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a likely sign of a diagnosis of aortic transection? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which sign is NOT a sign of aortic transection.

Obviously surgical emphysema is not unlikely in the overall setting of trauma however it is not a direct sign of aortic transection.

An aortic transection is highly likely to be next-to immediately fatal. Formation of a pseudoaneurysm at the transection site can sometimes contain extravasation but the scenario of a patient surviving long enough to receive even a chest x-ray otherwise seems a little far-fetched but does occur in exceptional circumstances. Disruption to the aortic contour and bilateral pleural effusions are given as signs of aortic transaction. The trachea is shifted to the right by mass effect from the enlarging haematoma around the aorta.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: Thoracic duct disruption at the level of T4
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a likely diagnosis.

Aspergillosis

Aspergillosis is an all encompassing term which refers to the spectrum of lung diseases caused by the fungus Aspergillus.  How the fungus affects the patient depends on their underlying immune status.

Severely immunocompromised patients                    → Invasive aspergillosis

Mildly immunocompromised patients                        → semi-invasive aspergillosis

Normal patients                                                               → non-invasive aspergillosis (such as colonization of a pre-existing cyst or cavity)

Hypersensitive patients (Cystic fibrosis or asthmatics) → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)

The halo sign is used to describe the appearance of a nodule surrounded by a ‘halo’ of ground glass opacification. It occurs when there is alveolar haemorrhage and is considered to be a classical finding in invasive aspergillosis.

ABPA causes a ‘migratory pneumonitis’, typically affecting the upper lobes. Parenchymal changes are fleeting; appearing in one area of the lung one week and a different area the next. The ‘finger in glove’ sign can often be seen, where mucus plugging of a bronchus allows the distal airway to fill with secretions giving rise to a ‘V’ or Y’ shaped shadow on a CXR or CT. Central bronchiectasis is a prominent feature and maybe indicated by the phrase ‘ring shadows’ in a description. The peripheral bronchi are classically spared. Cavity formation is seen in the later stages of the disease although aspergillomas are not typical (these occur in patients with a normal immune system). The typical patient will be young, with a history of either asthma or cystic fibrosis or ‘chronic lung disease’, symptoms of malaise, headache and intermittent chest pains, and an eosinophilia on their full blood count.

Boerhaave syndrome

Benign oesophageal rupture can occur during forceful vomiting and causes sudden chest pain. Most occur along the left-hand wall of the oesophagus and hence initially the most common finding is a left sided pleural effusion. Fluid escapes into the pleural cavity and although aspiration may have occurred during the vomiting, consolidation develops later on, if at all. Tertiary contractions refer to non-propulsive oesophageal contractions and are a feature of achalasia. If Boerhaave syndrome is suspected the patient should not receive oral barium since it can raise a fibrotic process in the pleura. Water soluble contrast media such as gastrograffin should be used instead.

Thoracic duct disruption

The thoracic duct is the entry point into the venous circulation of lymphatic drainage from the majority of the body. It crosses the midline at the level of T5/6 and then enters the venous circulation where the left subclavian vein meets the internal jugular vein. Transections above T5/6 will cause a left sided effusion whereas those occurring inferior to the midline-crossing cause a right sided pleural effusion. The effusion consists of chyle and will therefore be high in fat.

Traumatic aortic rupture

Traumatic aortic rupture is most likely to occur at the site of the ligamentum arteriosus, just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. This is termed the aortic isthmus. The proximal aorta is fixed by the ligamentum arteriosus but distal to this point the aorta is more freely mobile.

He undergoes a CT of his abdomen which shows this to be due to chronic constipation for which he is already taking many different laxatives. The radiologist also notices airspace consolidation to his lung bases bilaterally. In patches the airspace changes have Hounsfield units of around -10.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lipoid pneumonia

Lipoid pneumonia results from ingestion or inhalation of a fat rich substance. In an exam question setting this can be anything from cod liver oil given to children or oil based laxatives (as in this case), or flammable substances used by ‘fire-eaters’. There is a lower zone predominance with air-space shadowing. If fat-density is described in the question in any way (i.e. negative Hounsfield units) then this points strongly to a lipoid pneumonia. The patients can be asymptomatic.

Aspiration pneumonia

Gastric acid aspiration (Mendelson syndrome) causes a nasty chemical pneumonitis owing to the acidity of the gastric contents. This can cause a spectrum of issues ranging from a mild bronchiolitis to haemorrhagic pulmonary oedema depending on the extent of the aspiration. It some senses it is not the classical aspiration pneumonia as the affected lobes tend to be less ‘bibasal’ and more posterior or to the middle of the thorax reflecting a likely semi-reclined position of affected patients.

Boerhaave syndrome

This is oesophageal rupture with consequential extrusion of gastric contents into the pleural spaces and mediastinum. Management is usually surgical initially with many patients suffering a laborious recovery trajectory, often plagued by multitudes of complications lasting many years. Radiographically patients often have a pleural effusion at presentation, moreso on the left than the right.

Hamartoma

Fat within a thoracic mass is diagnostic of a hamartoma but is only seen in approximately half of cases.

Tuberculosis

TB has an increased prevalence in homeless communities and can present as a pneumonia with airspace opacification that fails to respond to empirical CAP (Community acquired pneumonia) antibiotic therapy. However in this question involvement of the dependant portion of the lung point more towards an aspiration pneumonia. In the real world however testing for TB while treating for an aspiration pneumonia would be sensible.

stem: A 40-year-old athlete complains of calf claudication. On Doppler ultrasound there is popliteal stenosis. He undergoes an MRA which shows a medial slip of the medial head of gastrocnemius.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (PAES)

This arises due to an anomalous anatomy of the muscles around the knee, for example when the insertion of the medial head of gastrocnemius is anomalous and compresses the popliteal artery leading to symptoms of claudication, particularly on exertion, in an otherwise fit individual. There are a number of different anomalous patterns which can cause PAES (e.g. lateral insertion of the medial head, fibrous band, accessory medial head etc). Of note, management is surgical; surgical release has far better outcomes than endovascular stenting.

Cystic adventitial degeneration

On MRI scanning, mucous cysts can be seen in the wall of the popliteal artery. These, like most cysts, show high T2 signal and the T1 signal can be variable depending on the quantity of mucin present. This disease has a strong male preponderance and particularly affects the popliteal artery. On MRI the signal can be variable on T1 depending on the protein content of the cyst but returns a high signal on T2.

Spinal cord stenosis

The inclusion of this answer pertains to symptoms of neurogenic claudication which can arise in the context of spinal cord stenosis or disc pathology, typically of the lumbar spine. Sensory and/or motor deficit at the appropriate level is found on neurological examination.

Buerger disease

This disease is strongly linked to smoking and manifests as a vasculitis of the smaller arteries. Arterial occlusion with the formation of corkscrew-shaped collaterals occurs initially in the small arteries of the hands and feet but becoming more proximal as the disease progresses. Of note the larger proximal and central arteries lack the calcification which would otherwise be seen with disease of this extent when caused by atherosclerosis.

prompt: Select one answer only.
options: RI difference between the kidneys of >5%
explanation:
There are three main aetiologies of renal artery stenosis. The most prevalent is atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is the second most common and is classically given as affecting a relatively young woman with beading (string of beads) of the mid and distal renal arteries seen, for which the management is angioplasty. Finally a small number of cases are secondary to a variety of conditions such as Buerger disease, Takayasu disease and neurofibromatosis.

The significance of diagnosis of atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is in avoiding the use of ACE inhibitors. The ASTRAL trial showed that there was no long term benefit of stenting the stenoses over best medical management, although there was still a reduction in the number of episodes of flash pulmonary oedema experienced by the patients.

There is conflicting literature about the use of resistive index in evaluating for renal artery stenosis in transplant kidneys. The normal value is around 0.7. Some studies have shown figures slightly higher than this (around 0.78) in mild-moderate renal artery stenosis but lower (0.6) in severe renal artery stenosis and in native kidneys studies have shown high resistive indices (above 0.7) to be associated with parenchymal scarring indicating the kidney may respond poorly to revascularisation therapy and resistive index is used to help inform treatment decisions on this basis. It is generally thought not to be a useful marker for diagnosis in renal artery stenosis though, in either native or transplant kidneys.

prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the inferior vena cava is true?
options: It arises as the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the L3 vertebral level
It directly receives a tributary from the right gonadal vein
It drains into the left atrium of the heart
It pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T10 vertebral level
explanation:
The inferior vena cava carries deoxygenated blood from all of the structures lying below the diaphragm into the right atrium of the heart. It arises as the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the L5 vertebral level.

It ascends upwards in the retroperitoneal space, to the right of the lumbar vertebral bodies and to the right of the aorta. It pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level to enter the thorax. It then almost immediately enters the pericardium before draining into the right atrium.

The inferior vena cava receives tributaries from:

Common iliac veins (origin at L5) – drain lower limbs and gluteal regions

Lumbar veins (between L1 and L5) – drain the posterior abdominal wall

Right gonadal vein (L2) – drain the right testis/ovary

Renal veins (L1) – drain the kidneys, left adrenal gland, left testis/ovary

Right adrenal vein (L1) – drains the right adrenal gland

Right, middle and left hepatic veins (T8) – drain the liver

Right and left inferior phrenic veins (T8) – drain the diaphragm

stem: A CT scan shows a nodule in a large cavity.
prompt: This is more likely to be malignant under which of the following circumstances?
explanation:
The main cavitating neoplastic culprits are:

Contrast enhancement in a nodule is a strong indicator of malignancy and vice versa is also true; the absence of contrast enhancement strongly suggests a nodule is benign. True dependancy (on both supine and prone scans) would be suggestive of aspergilloma formation. Volume loss suggests fibrosis.
