prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
An aortic aneurysm is simply a dilatation of the aorta. The vast majority of these will be degenerate, caused by longstanding atherosclerosis and hypertension. Connective tissue diseases such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos can predispose to aortic aneurysms at an earlier age. Fusiform aneurysmal dilatation is typical of a degenerate aneurysm.

An inflammatory aneurysm occurs when there is inflammation and fibrosis affecting the wall of the aorta. Fibrotic stricturing of the ureters with consequential hydronephrosis is classical and serves as an excellent differentiator from mycotic or degenerative aneurysms. They also occur in a slightly younger age bracket to degenerative aneurysms. Inflammatory aneurysms are associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis and thereby other IgG4-related diseases.

A mycotic aneurysm occurs when the integrity of the wall of the aorta is compromised by bacterial infection, usually spread from a source elsewhere within the body either haematogenously or by local spread. These aneurysms tend to be more saccular or multilobulated in morphology, reflecting the focal mural compromise. Adjacent soft tissue stranding is present and adjacent gas locules are almost pathognomonic albeit rare. This would be the second most likely diagnosis in this scenario.

A syphilitic aneurysm (also termed Luetic aneurysms), represents tertiary syphilis and therefore has a lag time of anywhere from 5 to 25 years from the initial infection. It occurs when the vasa vasorum supplying the wall of the aorta itself with blood becomes infected with the spirochete Treponema pallidum which causes syphilis. Although there has been a resurgence of syphilis in recent years it should be noted that many of the new cases are likely to be caught and treated long before tertiary syphilis develops.

IgG4 related diseases are one of Radiology’s newest entities. They comprise a constellation of fibrotic conditions affecting virtually every part of the body, mediated by a subclass of Immunoglobulin called IgG4. Where one condition exists others may also be present. The more common of these include:

Orbital pseudotumour

Fibrosing mediastinitis

Reidel thyroiditis

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Sclerosing mesenteritis

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

An elevated ESR and/or CRP is often seen.

stem: A 56-year-old man complaining of chest pain undergoes a CT chest that shows a 6cm hilar mass measuring 60HU which demonstrates modest enhancement post-contrast.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Carcinoid

These are low-grade lung malignancies with a good prognosis. They are usually central in location (in contrast to the peripheral preferences of hamartomas). Calcification is a common feature in approximately a third of cases which in this question is weakly suggested by the high attenuation. Typically carcinoids are very vascular tumours that enhance avidly, and usually derive their blood supply from the bronchial arteries rather than the pulmonary arteries. Atypical carcinoids can show less enhancement though at least 30 HU of net gain should be expected. An atypical carcinoid will also tend to be less well rounded and more aggressive in appearance. They are larger than typical carcinoids but otherwise it is difficult to distinguish between typical and atypical carcinoids; it is essemtially a histological diagnosis.

The carcinoid syndrome seen in abdominal carcinoids is far less commonly seen with thoracic carcinoids. Wheezing, on the other hand, can be given in an exam question setting as a feature to point towards endobronchial carcinoid lesions (i.e. mechanical obstruction).

Lymphoma

Lymphoma would be unlikely owing to the lack of enhancement.

Duplication cyst

A duplication cyst would have a much lower HU than 60 – it would be expected to be far closer to zero.

Neurofibroma

Although neurofibromas often show little enhancement on CT post contrast, again 60HU would be too high for most neurofibromas. Additionally a neurofibroma would more usually be described as having an intraspinal element. Dumbbell protrusion through the neural foramina.

explanation:
With the presence of fat density the diagnosis of hamartoma can be made and consequently no follow up is required.

Fat within a thoracic mass is diagnostic of a hamartoma but is only seen in approximately half of cases. In contradistinction to carcinoid tumours, hamartomas tend to be peripherally located whereas carcinoid tumours are often more central. Exceptions to both are reasonably frequent however. Calcification, especially popcorn calcification, is also very classical for hamartomas if present. Cavitation is not a feature often associated with them, but it can be found occasionally. Hamartomas form part of Carney triad (pulmonary chondromas, gastric leiomyosarcomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas). NB this is different from Carney complex (atrial myxoma, facial/buccal pigmentation, sertoli tumours of the testis and multiple other findings).

stem: You are reporting a lower limb angiogram for a patient with claudication.
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the posterior tibial artery is FALSE?
options: It arises at the trifurcation of the popliteal artery
It can be palpated on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
It carries blood to the posterior compartment of the leg
It is accompanied by the posterior tibial vein throughout its course
It terminates by bifurcating into the medial and lateral plantar arteries
explanation:
The posterior tibial artery arises at the so-called 'trifurcation' of the popliteal artery (or more accurately, at the bifurcation of the tibioperoneal artery, the anterior tibial artery having already been given off slightly more proximally) just beneath the fibrous arch of soleus, at the lower border of popliteus. It carries blood to the posterior compartment of the leg and the plantar surface of the foot.

The posterior tibial artery terminates by bifurcating into the medial and lateral plantar arteries deep to abductor hallucis. It is accompanied by a deep vein, the posterior tibial vein, throughout its course.

The posterior tibial artery pulse can be easily palpated posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus at Pimenta’s point. It is often examined at this point during the assessment of patients for the presence of peripheral vascular disease.

The pulse of the dorsalis pedis artery, not the posterior tibial artery, can be easily palpated on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

prompt: What is the most likely finding?
explanation:
Mitral regurgitation

Chronic regurgitation causes left atrial enlargement with splaying of the carina and a double right heart border. It is also the only valvular pathology associated with isolated right upper lobe pulmonary oedema.

Aortic stenosis

This can be congenital or acquired. Dilation of ascending aorta is seen due to a jet from the stenosis. Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is occasionally a feature.

Aortic regurgitation

This is usually secondary to bacterial endocarditis, Marfan’s, bicuspid aortic valve or aortic root dilatation (due to hypertension).

Mitral stenosis

The most common cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic heart disease. It can cause left atrial dilatation, but is not associated with right upper lobe pulmonary oedema.

Tricuspid regurgitation

This occurs with right ventricular strain, for example in the context of large pulmonary emboli. It is sometimes evident on CT as reflux of contrast into the hepatic veins.

stem: You are reporting a CTPA scan which has filling defects bilaterally in the pulmonary arteries.
prompt: Which of the following would favour a diagnosis of acute emboli over chronic emboli?
explanation:
Enlargement of the pulmonary arteries can be seen when there is severe right heart strain but an enlarged main pulmonary artery is more associated with chronic pulmonary emboli leading to pulmonary hypertension.

Contrast within the hepatic veins is seen when there is tricuspid regurgitation and can be seen in both acute and chronic pulmonary emboli.

The polo mint sign is seen when the CT slice is at 90o to the direction of flow in a given pulmonary artery.

The railway track sign is seen when the CT slice is in line with the direction of flow.

Eccentricity of the thrombus is more suggestive of a chronic pulmonary embolus. Acute emboli sit within the lumen of the artery and where they touch the wall of the artery will subtend an acute angle, whereas chronic emboli flatten against the walls of the artery in a crescenteric shape and thereby subtend an obtuse angle.

Bronchial artery collaterals form in the setting of chronic pulmonary emboli.

Acute pulmonary emboli

Filling defects within the pulmonary arteries can be seen on any post-contrast CT scans but a dedicated CT pulmonary angiogram has a higher sensitivity in this regard. The polo mint and railtrack signs are given as signs of acute pulmonary emboli. Acute emboli also sit within the lumen of the pulmonaries and therefore subtend an acute angle with the wall. When the clot load is haemodynamically significant features of right heart strain can be seen. These include bowing of the interventricular septum, right ventricular enlargement (the right ventricle should not be larger than the left ventricle). Dilatation of the main pulmonary artery (the main pulmonary artery should not be larger than the aorta). There are various features which can help determine the chronicity of an embolus or emboli. These are summarised in the table below:

Acute

Chronic

Tricuspid regurgitation – contrast in hepatic veins

Acute angles

Obtuse angles

Railway track sign

Bronchial artery collaterals

Polo mint sign

Webs and bands

CTEPH (Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension)

When acute pulmonary emboli fail to resolve there is a danger that their presence will lead to elevated pulmonary arterial pressures i.e CTEPH. The symptoms and radiological signs of CTEPH pertain either to the thrombi or the pulmonary hypertension. Filling defects on CTPA can be expected. Differentiating chronic from acute pulmonary emboli is not an exact science but chronic PEs can display features such as luminal eccentricity (build up of thrombus along the walls of the pulmonary arteries as opposed to central filling defects within the lumen) and calcification. Webs and bands are also features of chronicity - thin, threadlike fibrous structures attached at either end to the vessel wall but free-floating in their mid-portions. Features of the consequent pulmonary hypertension include enlargement of the main pulmonary arteries with stenosis of the peripheral arteries giving rise to a tapered appearance. Right ventricular enlargement and hypertrophy should also be looked for. The bronchial arteries derive from the aorta and thus provide a welcome opportunity for collateralisation thereby maintaining blood flow to lung segments where thrombus is chronically occluding the pulmonary artery.

prompt: What is the most accurate description of this abnormality?
explanation:
Myocardial scar / Chronic infarct

This is a non-reperfusable myocardial defect (chronic infarct). It gives a wall motion abnormality but would demonstrate thinned myocardium. The T2 signal is low. Scars demonstrate abnormal Thallium perfusion but does not redistribute with delayed thallium, and does not take up FDG.

Stunned myocardium

This gives a wall motion abnormality with high T2 signal. There is normal perfusion on Thallium or sestamibi scanning which is a key differentiating feature against hibernating myocardium. It should be expected to spontaneously resolve, whereas hibernating myocardium will not resolve spontaneously.

Hibernating myocardium

This can be seen as a wall motion abnormality, but also gives abnormal fixed perfusion. Hibernating myocardium redistributes delayed thallium and takes up FDG.

Focal myocarditis

This classically affects the mid-wall or epicardial (not subendocardial) and does not stay confined to a vascular territory.

stem: A 56-year-old man who has a history of intravenous drug use presents with severe back pain. He undergoes a CT scan which shows aortic pathology adjacent to a left psoas abscess.
prompt: Which of the following imaging findings is most likely to be seen?
explanation:
A mycotic aneurysm occurs when the integrity of the wall of the aorta is compromised by bacterial infection, usually spread from a source elsewhere within the body either haematogenously or by local spread. These aneurysms tend to be more saccular or multilobulated in morphology, reflecting the focal mural compromise. Adjacent soft tissue stranding is present and adjacent gas locules are almost pathognomonic, albeit rare.

An aortic aneurysm is simply a dilatation of the aorta. The vast majority of these will be degenerate, caused by longstanding atherosclerosis and hypertension. Connective tissue diseases such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos can predispose to aortic aneurysms at an earlier age. Fusiform aneurysmal dilatation is typical of a degenerate aneurysm.

Pseudoaneurysm formation occurs when there is rupture through one or more of the layers of an artery but there is containment of the rupture either by the adventitial layer or surrounding soft tissues. They are commonly either traumatic or iatrogenic in aetiology. Mycotic aneurysms can become pseudoaenurysmal.

stem: A 31-year-old lady with a history of cystic fibrosis presents with worsening shortness of breath and a cough. She underwent a bilateral lung transplant 8 years previously. An HRCT is requested which shows bilateral ground glass opacities with air trapping on the expiratory phases.
prompt: What is the most likely cause? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome

There are two very similarly named syndromes which are completely different in aetiology  but frequently confused.

BOOP – bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia. This is the old term for what is now referred to as COP (Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia). There is patchy consolidation and ground glass opacification.

BOS – bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome. This is part of a CLAD (chronic lung allograft dysfunction). In CLAD, a transplanted lung is not being rejected (another common misnomer) but the graft is undergoing fibrosis which causes respiratory dysfunction. The findings on CT, in the case of BOS, include mosaic attenuation with air trapping, bronchial wall thickening and bronchiectasis.

Post-transplant complications

The radiology of post-transplant lungs may be niche but it is important, particularly in the early post-operative days. Post-transplant complications can be, in an exam question setting at least, alluded to on the basis of their time frame.

Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is known as the great mimic as it can appear in almost any way it chooses. Classical thoracic sarcoidosis is seen as perilymphatic nodules and interlobular septal thickening in association with mediastinal and hilar lymph node enlargement. Eggshell calcification is a feature often associated with sarcoidosis and does become increasingly common with disease duration but still only affects a fifth of patients.

Among features not typical of sarcoidosis, pleural disease (including pleural effusion) is important to note and should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses where present. Similarly, cavitation of lymph nodes is also atypical.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HSP) also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA)

This condition is caused by a granulomatous reaction to an inhaled allergen. Consequently, it is the upper zones which are most affected. A detailed history should reveal the source of an antigen e.g. malt farmer, bird fancier, proximity to air conditioners etc. On CT EAA appears as widespread patchy ground glass opacification, mosaic in nature with nodules in a centrilobular distribution. Fibrosis and consequential volume loss occur over months-years of allergen exposure. Involvement of the pleura (including pleural effusions) is very rare which can separate this condition from many others.

MAC – mycobacterium avium complex

This is an atypical mycobacterial infection is often seen in the form of Lady Windermere syndrome. Classically there is bronchiectasis and tree-in-bud in the right middle lobe which is affected in isolation from the rest of the lung and the patient is usually an otherwise perfectly healthy Caucasian elderly woman. Lady Windermere is the central character in a play by Oscar Wilde. The play was written in an era where it would have been considered impolite and unpleasant to cough. The term applies to a form of MAC infection thought to result from voluntary suppression of the kind of cough which would usually be expected with the airway irritation brought on a pathogen. Where MAC occurs in not otherwise healthy individuals there is an association with any disease causing bronchiectasis.

Aspergillosis

Of the different varieties of pulmonary aspergillosis it is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) which is most associated with the tree-in-bud appearance. This occurs due to hypersensitivity towards aspergillus spp and is seen in asthmatics or, less commonly, patients with cystic fibrosis. Hypersensitivity reactions give rise to bronchial wall oedema and the broncho-alveolar lumen becomes filled with fluid. Superimposed mucous impaction is also a feature. Owing to the inhalational element of pathogen exposure there is a predisposition for the upper lobes.

The interface of the right lung and mediastinal reflection of the azygos vein
The interface of the right lung and posterior mediastinal soft tissue
The opposition of the pleural surfaces of the posteromedial surfaces of the upper lobes posteriorly to the oesophagus
The right tracheal wall adjacent to the pleural surface
explanation:
The azygo-oesophageal recess is formed by the interface of the right lung and the mediastinal reflection of the azygos vein.

The anterior junctional line is formed by the meeting of the parietal and visceral pleura anteromedially.

The posterior junctional line is formed by the meeting of the pleural surfaces of the upper lobes behind the oesophagus.

The right paratracheal line is formed by the right wall of the trachea against the right lung.

stem: A 78-year-old lady has a new diagnosis of lung cancer. There is a 3cm mass lesion touching the right main bronchus in the right upper lobe. No chest wall invasion is seen but there is a second smaller lesion in the lingula. Enlarged lymph nodes are seen in the ipsilateral mediastinum only. There is no pleural effusion.
prompt: Which of the following denotes the poorest prognosis?
explanation:
For this patient the presence of a satellite nodule in a contralateral lobe is considered as metastatic disease.

In an ideal world every trainee radiologist would have all the intricacies of staging for all tumour types committed to memory. A qualified subspecialist radiologist could reasonably be expected to be extremely familiar with the staging for cancers within their remit but for the majority of trainees it is simply not practical to memorise each and every staging scheme. As an overall strategy, the most important stages to understand are those which change the management for patients. Of note with lung cancer, at Stage IIIb the management changes significantly because stage IIIb and stage IV patients are unresectable. Another useful facet to lung cancer (TNM) staging is satellite nodules:

Same lobe = T3

Different lobe = T4

Contralateral lung = M1

For lung cancer some of the important staging features are as follows (IASLC 8th ed):

T1 tumours are <3cm

N1 = ipsilateral hilar nodes

T2 tumours are 3-5cm but dont involve the carina

N2 = ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal nodes

T3 tumours are 5-7cm OR with extension to:

Chest wall

Diaphgragm

Pericardium

Satellite nodules within the same lobe

N3 = contralateral hilar, mediastinal or supraclavicular nodes

M1 = bilateral lesions, malignant pleural effusion, distant metastases

T4 tumours affect mediastinal organs, carina, vertebral body

T1 and T2 both have further subdivisions.

Unresectable tumours are T4, N3 or M1.

Beyond TNM staging patients with similar prognostic outcomes are given further stages. Simple observation of these groupings reveals the following:

Stage I patients MUST be N0

Stage III patients MUST have a sum ≥ 3 (ie T2N2M0, or T1N2M0). [NB some patients with Stage II will also have a sum of 3 (for example T2N1M0) however ALL stage III patients have a sum ≥ 3.]

Stage IIIb patients are unresectable → stage IIIb is denoted either by N3 status or T4N2.

stem: A 40-year-old man undergoes a CT scan of his chest. This shows thickening of the pericardium measuring around 5mm. The right ventricle is small and there is straightening of the interventricular septum. Ascites can be seen in the included upper abdomen.
prompt: What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Constrictive pericarditis

Inflammation of the pericardium is termed pericarditis and leads to fibrous thickening. Most commonly this occurs either post-operatively in patients undergoing cardiac surgery or as an idiopathic entity although historically it was tuberculosis which was the most common cause of pericarditis. The diagnosis is predominantly clinical with symptoms such as malaise or dyspnoea and signs such as neck vein distension or paradoxical movement of the JVP. On cross sectional imaging thickening of the pericardium to greater than 2mm can be seen and the fibrosis causes a restriction in distensibility. The right ventricle, being more compliant than the left, becomes flattened and furthermore there can be straightening or curvature of the septum towards the left. Elsewhere, if the field of view permits, accessory signs such as pleural effusions and even ascites may be seen.

Infectious pericarditis

Enhancement of the pericardium suggests active inflammation. Locules of gas within a pericardial effusion suggest the presence of gas forming organisms, though these are rarely seen. Fat stranding may be seen within the fat of the adjacent mediastinum.

Pulmonary Emboli

There is some cross-over of the signs and symptoms of pericarditis and a large lobar embolus. On CT, if the embolus is large enough to cause right ventricular strain the septum can sometimes appear bowed with reflux of IV contrast into the hepatic veins.

Aortic dissection

Dissections are classified according to their involvement of the aortic root and their distal extent. There are two different classification systems. The Stanford classification is more useful clinically since the primary decision post-diagnosis is whether the dissection will be managed surgically or medically. Those involving the proximal aorta and arch are managed surgically. If the arch is not involved, the patient can be managed medically. Thus, Stanford A dissections involve the aorta proximal to the origin of the left subclavian artery with or without concurrent distal involvement. Stanford B dissections do not involve the proximal aorta. Where a dissection extends proximally and causes pericardial tamponade the clinical signs and symptoms may well occur, however the presence of effusions and pitting oedema do not fit with the correct answer being aortic dissection.

stem: A 25-year-old lady with chest pain, dyspnoea and weight loss undergoes a CXR which shows a widened mediastinum. A subsequent CT shows a lobulated 8cm anterior mediastinal mass. The clerking doctor notices a raised LDH on the initial blood results.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The ‘5Ts’ of anterior mediastinal masses are a useful aide memoire:

Thymoma

Thyroid tumours

Teratoma

Thoracic aorta

Terrible lymphoma

Malignant germ cell tumour

These include seminomas and non-seminomatous (embryonal, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma, mixed cell type) tumours. Generally speaking they affect young adults and an elevated hCG, LDH, or alpha fetoprotein is usually present. The presence of effusions suggests local pleural invasion and may well be seen. Although the presence or absence of calcification is not featured in this question, the lack of calcification is in-keeping with seminomatous tumours.

Malignant thymoma

These tumours spread by invading the mediastinum and encasing the lung with pleural thickening. Vascular invasion is also seen. There is an association with myasthenia gravis, hence the features of weakness and fatigue symptoms with lid lag and diplopia also commonly described. Pleural deposits are also a good feature to suggest a malignant thymoma over some of the other possible options.

Hodgkin lymphoma

Hodgkin lymphoma has two age peaks in prevalence, one in the late 20s and one in the late 70s. It can present at any age however. If a histological finding of Reed-Sternberg cells (binucleate white cells) is given there can be no other diagnosis. Hodgkin lymphoma tends to cause anterior mediastinal masses whereas Non-hodgkin lymphoma tends to cause posterior mediastinal masses. Hodgkin lymphoma nodal involvement spreads contiguously from one region to the next. This makes the staging very easy to remember.

Stage I = one nodal group involved

Stage II = two or more nodal groups involved on the same side of the diaphragm

Stage III = nodal groups on either side of the diaphragm

Stage IV = involvement of non-lymphatic structures (e.g. bone or lung)

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL)

NHL is 4 times more prevalent than Hodgkin lymphoma. Thoracic lymph node enlargement is common and classically affects the posterior mediastinum. Unlike Hodgkin lymphoma, NHL demonstrates non-contiguous spread and thus the whole neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis should be included in staging imaging.

Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

Mediastinal nodes

Anterior

Non-contiguous

Predominantly

Thorax

Abdomen

Approx 4%

Approx 85%

Approx 50%

Lipoma

Lipomas are usually easily distinguished by their fat content, giving negative Hounsfield units. No Hounsfield units have been provided here but the remainder of the clinical information provided would not be explained by a lipoma.

explanation:
The pulmonary arteries receive deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle and deliver it to the lungs.

The pulmonary arteries begin as the short and wide pulmonary trunk at the base of the right ventricle. It is separated from the right ventricle by the pulmonary valve and is located anteriorly and medially to the right atrium.

The ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk twist around each other, with the aorta initially lying posterior to the pulmonary trunk, before twisting to the right and lying anteriorly to it.

The pulmonary trunk divides into the left and right pulmonary arteries. The left pulmonary artery supplies blood to the left lung and further divides into two separate arteries to supply each lobe of the lung. The right pulmonary artery is thicker and longer than the left and supplies blood to the right lung. It also bifurcates into two arteries, despite providing a blood supply to three lobes.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with bilateral renal resections for APCKD and a subsequent renal transplant has been anuric for 12 hours. She is about to be started on dialysis but her fistula is not working satisfactorily.
prompt: What is the best management option?
explanation:
This is a slightly frustrating question owing to the paucity of clinical information. Clearly if the patient becomes obtunded with a rising serum potassium then the priority would be filtration and thus central line placement to facilitate dialysis would be correct. Arguable this is the safest answer. However, in all likelihood this question is attempting to glean the candidates understanding of the usefulness of interventional radiology in such circumstances. Certainly it might be possible to salvage the fistula with angioplasty, which would undoubtedly be the best option for the patient, assuming they are fit enough to postpone dialysis until the procedure has been attempted. Anuria in a renal transplant patient for 12 hours would be cause for concern but would not, on its own, be a criterion for immediate dialysis.

Ultrasound guided needle placement may facilitate dialysis in a working fistula, but does not address the flow within the fistula if this is unsatisfactory. Surgical exploration of the fistula may also produce a successful outcome but is a more invasive procedure. CAPD (Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis) is not suitable in the acute setting.

stem: You are reporting the CT scan of an 80 year old man. There are confluent pleural calcifications on the left, with a calcified lymph node in the AP window. There is sparing of the costophrenic angle.
prompt: What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Asbestosis is not a likely cause of mediastinal lymph node calcification. The differential diagnosis for this finding is given below.

When calcified pleural plaques are seen bilaterally it is virtually pathognomonic of prior asbestos exposure. Of all asbestos related pleural plaques around 85% are calcified. Involvement of the mediastinal pleura should raise the possibility of mesothelioma but involvement of the costophrenic angles should raise the possibility of an alternative diagnosis as these are usually spared in asbestos related plaque disease. Sparing can occur in other pathologies too and should not be taken as an absolute sign of asbestosis, merely that involvement of the costophrenic angles suggests an alternative diagnosis. Unilateral pleural plaques can be caused by any previous insult such as surgery or an empyema although the most common cause is still asbestos related lung disease.

Mediastinal lymph node calcification

This can be seen in a number of conditions:

Tuberculosis

Histoplasmosis

Amyloidosis (rare)

Metastases: papillary/medullary thyroid cancer, osteosarcoma, mucinous adenocarcinoma

Specifically egg-shell calcification

Silicosis and coal workers pneumoconiosis

Sarcoidosis

Treated lymphoma

prompt: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for beta-blocker administration?
explanation:
Contraindications to beta-blocker administration.

Asthmatics - Generally only brittle asthmatics are contraindicated from having beta blockers. If they have had previous ITU admissions or recent hospital admissions, beta-blockers should be used with extreme caution.

Heart-block - 1st degree block is acceptable. 2nd and 3rd degree blocks are absolute contraindications.

Sildenafil - use within 48 hours of a cardiac CT is a contraindication to GTN administration, but not beta-blocker administration.

Profound anaemia is a contraindication to GTN administration, but beta blockers are not contra-indicated.

Mitral regurgitation is not a contraindication. Aortic stenosis is a contraindication to GTN administration and a relative contraindication to beta blocker use too.

FDG imaging relies on glucose uptake being increased in tissues of interest which are more metabolically active than non-target tissues. Hence the patient must be fasted such that the FDG given is taken up rapidly enough to produce an image.

FDG is renally excreted. Patients with a poor renal function are at risk of enduring a higher dose than those with a normal renal function. However, assuming the dose is correctly adjusted down there is no reason such patients cannot undergo PET/CT scanning.

Insulin treatment does not preclude imaging, and indeed helps reduce the extracellular glucose concentration thereby improving the quality of scans acquired later. There should be at least a 4-hour gap between the last insulin dose and the FDG tracer dose time.

The literature on fasting varies and different organizations have suggested slightly different fasting windows. The most conservative of these is 6 hours.

Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine must be avoided for at least 12 hours prior to the scan.

Exercise should be avoided for 24, if not 48 hours prior to the scan.

On a CT scan there is a linear lucency running through an area of ground glass shadowing. He goes on to have a PET CT scan which does not show avidity.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (MIA)

The term bronchalveolar carcinoma (BAC) is historic and shouldn't really be being used. Early on they appear as tiny areas of ground glass opacification (GGO). This then becomes more defined as a small nodule, sometimes still surrounded by a rim of GGO and termed the ‘fried egg’ sign. Air bronchograms can be seen within a small patch of consolidation, such as in this case. Unlike most other types of lung malignancy, PET/CT is often negative for such cases. Also unlike many other types of lung malignancy the incidence of AIS and MIA is higher in non-smokers. It also affects women more commonly than men (despite the demographics given in this question).

CMV pneumonia

Infection with CMV is common among AIDS patients but not all cases are diagnosed prior to the autopsy prevalence of over 50%; it does not cause significant morbidity or mortality. When it does manifest radiologically the findings are relatively non-specific with bronchiectasis, nodules and hazy infiltrates seen in a bilateral symmetrical distribution. It is often diagnosed concurrently with Kaposi sarcoma. As a cause of the tree-in-bud appearance it is unusual because the luminal opacification is derived from bronchial wall thickening as opposed to an exogenous substance. Changes are usually widespread; there is no particular predilection for the middle lobe. There can be significant overlap between the appearances of CMV pneumonia and PCP. The main differences to look for would be an apical predominance for PCP (especially in those taking prophylactic pentamidine), and the presence of cysts in PCP.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) also known as Bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP)

COP is seen in patients post-infection, post-transplant, with a drug toxicity (chemo or methotrexate among others) or in an idiopathic setting. Patients experience a flu-like illness and a dry cough with worsening dyspnoea dating back over the preceding few months. Patients are often treated initially as a bacterial pneumonia and unsurprisingly there is then no response to antibiotic therapy. On CT there is patchy consolidation or ground glass opacification (GGO) and a third of patients will have pleural effusions or lymph node enlargement.

The reverse halo appearance is synonymous with COP (also known as BOOP – Bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia). It is seen as central ground glass opacification surrounded by a ring of consolidation. There are other conditions which can cause this appearance, of which the prominent ones are:

Wegeners granulomatosis

Sarcoidosis

Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia

Non-specific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP)

This is sometimes seen as a collection of left-over conditions which do not fit into under the banners of COP or UIP but is a specific entity in its own right. It can occur in association with the collagen vasculitides (Scleroderma, Sjogren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis and the like). Non-specific symptoms such as shortness of breath with a dry cough gradually worsen over a period of a few months and on HRCT there will be bilateral symmetrical ground glass opacification with microcystic honeycombing. Radiological changes are seen in a more peripheral distribution and the term ‘subpleural sparing’ is often used since the area immediately adjacent to the pleura can be relatively disease free. The architectural distortion is said to be less with NSIP than with IPF (Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) and the patients tend to be slightly younger. NSIP usually responds well to steroid therapy.

Eosinophilic pneumonitis

This term includes a number of related conditions.

Simple pulmonary eosinophilia – also known as Loeffler syndrome – The key to the radiological findings in this syndrome is nodules with a ground glass opacification (GGO) halo. These nodules are said to be transient or migratory with resolution in some areas but new development in others as seen on serial scans. Like most other entities which include eosinophilia, patients commonly have an atopic background such as asthma or eczema.

Acute eosinophilic pneumonia – The eosinophils are found in bronchoalveolar lavage as opposed to the blood in this condition. The patients tend to be relatively young adults who present with a short history of a few days of fever and myalgia. HRCT shows patchy GGO in a bilateral distribution. Patients respond well to steroid therapy

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia – The significance of the HRCT findings of this condition (in the context of an exam question) is that it gives a ‘reversed bat-wing appearance’ (Differential diagnosis: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia, sarcoidosis, resolving pulmonary oedema). Eosinophils are found both in the bronchoalveolar lavage as well as in the blood. Although patients often have an atopic history already, a diagnosis of adult-onset asthma is commonly seen. HRCT findings include bilateral non-segmental consolidation in the peripheries (hence reverse batwing). There is usually a rapid resolution with corticosteroids.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome – this can be diagnosed where there is an absence of any known cause of eosinophilia with evidence of organ dysfunction such as restrictive cardiomyopathy or interstitial pulmonary opacities.

Empyema

Normal central bronchi

aspergilloma

pneumothorax

explanation:
Aspergillomas, pneumothoraces, normal central bronchi and empyemas would all be atypical for ABPA.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is part of the spectrum of lung diseases caused by the fungus Aspergillus. How the fungus affects the patient depends on their underlying immune status.

Severely immunocompromised patients                    → Invasive aspergillosis

Mildly immunocompromised patients                        → semi-invasive aspergillosis

Normal patients                                                               → non-invasive aspergillosis (such as colonization of a pre-existing cyst or cavity)

Hypersensitive patients (Cystic fibrosis or asthmatics) → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

ABPA causes a ‘migratory pneumonitis’, typically affecting the upper lobes. Parenchymal changes are fleeting; appearing in one area of the lung one week and a different area the next. The ‘finger in glove’ sign can often be seen, where mucus plugging of a bronchus allows the distal airway to fill with secretions giving rise to a ‘V’ or Y’ shaped shadow on a CXR or CT. Central bronchiectasis is a prominent feature and maybe indicated by the phrase ‘ring shadows’ in a description. The peripheral bronchi are classically spared. Cavity formation is seen in the later stages of the disease although aspergillomas are not typical (these occur in patients with a normal immune system). The typical patient will be young, with a history of either asthma or cystic fibrosis or ‘chronic lung disease’, symptoms of malaise, headache and intermittent chest pains, and an eosinophilia on their full blood count.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to his GP with a persistent cough and a wheeze. He subsequently undergoes a CT scan which shows a solitary 2cm endobronchial polypoid mass with late arterial enhancement. A PET/CT scan shows this to have no uptake.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
All the answers given would be in the differential diagnosis for endobronchial lesions, with the addition of bronchogenic adenocarcinomas and squamous cell papillomas.

An arterially enhancing lesion suggests a carcinoid tumour – this is a classic feature for them.

More often than not bronchial carcinoid tumours show no uptake on PET. A small percentage (5%) of hamartomas are endobronchial but although they can be negative on PET too, arterial phase enhancement is not a feature.

stem: A 40-year-old man with dyspnoea, weight loss, cough and haemoptysis presents to his GP. He is tachypnoeic at rest with crepitations on auscultation. His blood tests are normal. A CT of his chest shows bilateral patchy hazy opacification and crazy-paving pattern. There is sparse patchy consolidation. No lymph nodes are present, there is not cardiomegaly or effusions. A biopsy shows a normal interstitium but alveoli filled with lipid and proteinacious material.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Crazy paving

This is the term given to the appearance of interlobular septal thickening on a background of patchy ground glass opacification (GGO). In an exam question setting it is strongly indicative of alveolar proteinosis simply because most patients with alveolar proteinosis do have a crazy paving pattern but crazy paving does does occur in a variety of other conditions:

Alveolar proteinosis

Acute respiratory distress syndrome

Goodpasture syndrome

Cryptogenic organising pneumonia (COP)

Sarcoidosis

Alveolar proteinosis

Overproduction of surfactant and/or reduced efficiency of clearance mechanisms result in accumulation of proteinaceous surfactant in the air spaces. It is a rare condition of young or middle aged adults and there is a strong association with smoking. The classic description for the CT signs seen with alveolar proteinosis is a crazy paving pattern. This is caused by the combination of interlobular septal thickening and patchy ground glass opacification. This is seen in a perihilar (also known as batwing) distribution. Of note there is no association with lymph node enlargement or effusions.

Goodpasture syndrome

This is an autoimmune disease caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies. The alveolar membrane also falls victim to circulating auto-antibodies. Patients present as adolescents or young adults with glomerulonephritis and haemoptysis. Bilateral consolidation changes can be seen on imaging which characteristically become reticular over the ensuing few weeks. This is due to organisation of the pulmonary haemorrhage and can appear as a crazy paving pattern.

Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis

Pulmonary haemosideration refers to the deposition of iron within the lungs. This can be secondary to a cause of lung haemorrhage such as Goodpasture syndrome or can be idiopathic. There is symmetrical involvement of the lower zones with a progression to a nodular/linear pattern.

Sarcoidosis

‘The great mimic’. In the real world sarcoidosis can appear as almost anything, almost anywhere. Despite this, there are usual ways for sarcoidosis to appear and these are more likely to be tested in exam questions. The classic patient for pulmonary sarcoidosis is young, female and black with hypercalcaemia. Raised ACE (Angiotensin-converting enzyme) levels should make you think of sarcoidosis, as should a positive Kveim-Siltzbach test (an intracutaneous injection of a suspension of human sarcoid spleen or lymph nodes). Nine out of ten patients with sarcoidosis will have some of thoracic manifestation. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is typical. There are many features considered classical for sarcoidosis:

The ‘1, 2, 3’ sign is present in at least three quarters of patients. It is also called the Garland triad or the pawnbroker's sign and refers to a specific pattern of lymph node enlargement involving both hilar nodes as well as the right paratracheal nodes.

Egg-shell calcification of lymph nodes - this is not exclusive to sarcoidosis but is seen in increasing numbers of patients as the disease duration increases

Traction bronchiectasis.

Upper lobe predominance.

Nodules - these are usually in a perilymphatic distribution but are also found elsewhere. Cavitation can occur but is not typical.

stem: A 64-year-old man with multiple myeloma presents with shortness of breath and ankle swelling. He undergoes a cardiac MRI scan. This shows diffuse enhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The information available in the vignette is sparse. In a patient with a known history of multiple myeloma, amyloidosis should always be considered. Without further details of the nature/location of the enhancement, there is nothing to dissuade the candidate from this option.

Amyloid cardiomyopathy

Amyloidosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning there is global enhancement of the endocardium, and on echocardiogram the myocardium takes on a characteristic granular and speckled appearance. In an exam question setting a history of multiple myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease or similar may be given to suggest secondary amyloidosis.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Sarcoidosis cardiomyopathy

Involvement of the myocardium is relatively rare in sarcoidosis. Inflammation causes myocardial scarring of the interventricular septum and left ventricle most commonly. This shows as epicardial or midwall delayed hyperenhancement on MRI. The patient in this question is certainly of an appropriate demographic for sarcoidosis. The main differential diagnoses would be myocarditis or Chagas disease based on imaging findings alone.

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy

The blood supply to the heart muscle itself is of interest here. The endocardium derives its blood directly from the chambers whereas the layer referred to as the subendocardium receives blood from the terminal branches of the coronary vessels. By the time they reach the subendocardium these blood vessels are small enough that ventricular contraction causes a degree of compression. The end result is that the subendocardium is particularly vulnerable to ischaemia, a fact which manifests in the delayed hyperenhancement patterns seen on MRI; ischaemic cardiomyopathy is seen as subendocardial delayed hyperenhancement or in more extreme cases transmural hyperenhancement. The pattern of hyperenhancement is also territorial with ischaemic cardiomyopathy, depending on which vessel(s) has been affected.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

HCM can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion; there are a number of specific different gene mutations which have been identified to cause cardiac myocardial hypertrophy. The most common category is asymmetrical hypertrophy, accounting for around two thirds of cases. Here the interventricular septum is markedly enlarged. The remaining third of cases display symmetrical/concentric hypertrophy or apical hypertrophy. Patients are younger than most of those with ischaemic cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning midwall hyperenhancement at the junction between the right and left ventricles is typical.

Alcoholic cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy occurs in patients with a history of alcohol abuse. There is dilation of both ventricles alongside thinning of the myocardium which appears hypokinetic on dynamic studies. Myocardial fibrosis occurs and because this typically affects the mid-myocardium it can be differentiated from ischaemic cardiomyopathy which is often transmural and confined to vascular territories. The different areas show delayed enhancement on MRI scans.

prompt: What is the SINGLE most likely explanation?
explanation:
Complications of asthma

The question is to do with the complications of asthma.

Air trapping is a well-known phenomenon in asthma and is seen as flattening of the hemi diaphragms and hypertransradiancy.

Superadded infection can complicate any respiratory condition and asthma is no exception.

ABPA is a known complication of asthma

Pneumothoraces and pneumomediastinum can complicate asthma although the incidence is actually not vastly higher than that in the general population.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis classically mimics asthma on a chest radiograph. In a known asthmatic this would be an unusual finding compared to the common complications listed above.

explanation:
Please note that the vignette describes a venous bleeding point.

Arterial bleeding from pelvic fractures

Pelvic fractures in the context of trauma are a cause of significant morbidity and mortality. Life threatening haemorrhage may be caused by arterial bleeding or other sources such as the fractured bones themselves, and the pelvic venous structures. External fixation is one of the few means of managing acute haemorrhage in the pre-hospital setting however for arterial bleeding it is far less effective at tamponading ongoing haemorrhage. It remains the treatment of choice for bone bleeding or venous bleeding.

Catheter angiography and embolisation is the most effective method to control arterial haemorrhage. If the patient is haemodynamically unstable due to an arterial pelvic haemorrhage, catheter embolisation still provides the best hope for managing the patient successfully. Even if the patient has abdominal injuries which are likely to necessitate open abdominal trauma surgery, studies have shown that arterial pelvic bleeding should still be controlled via catheter embolisation prior to their open surgery.

How the fungus aspergillus affects a patient depends on their underlying immune status.

Invasive aspergillosis is one of the ways in which the fungus aspergillus can affect the lungs. Although this is a different process to the creation of a Monod sign (air crescent at the superior aspect of an aspergilloma) they can seem similar.

The halo sign is used to describe the appearance of a nodule surrounded by a ‘halo’ of ground glass opacification. It occurs when there is alveolar haemorrhage and is considered to be a classical finding in invasive aspergillosis. It is also seen in a number of other conditions:

Haemorrhagic metastases – Malignant melanoma, choriocarcinoma, osteosarcoma, angiosarcoma

Bronchioalveolar carcinoma (now called minimally invasive adenocarcinoma)

Other fungal infections

Mycobacterial infections (TB and atypicals)

Wegener granulomatosis

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

ABPA

The peripheral bronchi are classically spared. A CT scan is performed which shows he has a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm.
prompt: At which vertebral level does the superior mesenteric artery arise from the abdominal aorta? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The abdominal aorta is the largest artery in the abdominal cavity. It arises as a continuation of the thoracic aorta as it passes posterior to the median arcuate ligament of the diaphragm at the T12 vertebral level.

It descends caudally in the retroperitoneal space, anterior and to the left of the lumbar vertebral bodies and to the left of the inferior vena cava.

It is approximately 13 cm long and ends slightly to the left of the midline at the L4 vertebral level where it bifurcates into the right and left common iliac arteries.

The abdominal aorta has three main groups of branches:

1. Single ventral gut arteries:

Coeliac artery (T12) – supplies the stomach, abdominal oeseophagus, liver, spleen, superior pancreas, and superior duodenum

Superior mesenteric artery (L1) – supplies the distal duodenum, jejunum. Ileum, ascending colon and part of the transverse colon

Inferior mesenteric artery (L3) – supplies the large intestine from the splenic flexure to the upper part of the rectum

2. Paired visceral arteries:

Middle adrenal arteries (L1) – supply the adrenal glands

Renal arteries (L2) – supply the kidneys

Gonadal arteries (L2/L3) – supply the testicles/ovaries

3. Paired wall arteries:

Inferior phrenic arteries (T12) – supply the diaphragm

Four paired lumbar arteries (between L1 and L4) – supply the abdominal wall and spinal cord

It also gives off one single unpaired parietal artery, the median sacral artery, at the L4 vertebral level.

He mentions that his father had passed away from a large heart attack aged 45.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

HCM can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion; there are a number of specific different gene mutations which have been identified to cause cardiac myocardial hypertrophy. The most common category is asymmetrical hypertrophy, accounting for around two thirds of cases. Here the interventricular septum is markedly enlarged. The remaining third of cases display symmetrical/concentric hypertrophy or apical hypertrophy. Patients are younger than most of those with ischaemic cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning midwall hyperenhancement at the junction between the right and left ventricles is typical.

Sarcoidosis cardiomyopathy

Involvement of the myocardium is relatively rare in sarcoidosis. Inflammation causes myocardial scarring of the interventricular septum and left ventricle most commonly. This shows as epicardial or midwall delayed hyperenhancement on MRI.

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy

The blood supply to the heart muscle itself is of interest here. The endocardium derives its blood directly from the chambers whereas the layer referred to as the subendocardium receives blood from the terminal branches of the coronary vessels. By the time they reach the subendocardium these blood vessels are small enough that ventricular contraction causes a degree of compression. The end result is that the subendocardium is particularly vulnerable to ischaemia, a fact which manifests in the delayed hyperenhancement patterns seen on MRI; ischaemic cardiomyopathy is seen as subendocardial delayed hyperenhancement or in more extreme cases transmural hyperenhancement. The pattern of hyperenhancement is also territorial with ischaemic cardiomyopathy, depending on which vessel(s) has been affected.

Amyloid cardiomyopathy

Amyloidosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. On MRI scanning there is global enhancement of the endocardium, and on echocardiogram the myocardium takes on a characteristic granular and speckled appearance. In an exam question setting a history of multiple myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn disease or similar may be given to suggest secondary amyloidosis.

Alcoholic cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy occurs in patients with a history of alcohol abuse. There is dilation of both ventricles alongside thinning of the myocardium which appears hypokinetic on dynamic studies. Myocardial fibrosis occurs and because this typically affects the mid-myocardium it can be differentiated from ischaemic cardiomyopathy which is often transmural and confined to vascular territories. The different areas show delayed enhancement on MRI scans.

stem: An 85-year-old man who has been a lifelong smoker is found to have lymphangitis carcinomatosis on a CT scan.
prompt: What is the most likely primary?
explanation:
There are four pieces of information given to us in this question on which to base our answer.

The patient is male

The patient is elderly

The patient is a heavy smoker

The patient has lymphangitis carcinomatosis

Of the cancers listed only pancreatic, lymphoma or adrenal cancers have any association with smoking and of these it is pancreatic cancer which stands out as the most closely associated. The patient is certainly in an appropriate demographic for pancreatic cancer. Furthermore, alongside thyroid cancer, pancreatic cancer is the most widely appreciated of those provided to cause lymphangitis carcinomatosis. The final piece of evidence to consider is that in terms of population statistics pancreatic cancer and lymphoma (non-Hodgkin lymphoma) have the highest incidence among those listed.

Lymphangitis carcinomatosis is easy to recognize on a scan but can be described in a number of different ways on paper. It occurs when tumour cells, spread via the lymphatics, accumulate in the connective tissues of the lung, in particular the interlobular septa. The classical description is as a smooth thick reticular polygonal network.

A mnemonic for the likely cancers is: Certain Cancers Spread By Plugging The Lymphatics (this is not an exclusive list). Of these Breast accounts for just over half of cases and gastric cancer accounts for most of the remainder.

Cervix Colon Stomach Breast Pancreas Thyroid Larynx (or lung – bronchogenic) Next  Diffuse calcific densities on chest x-ray A 56-year-old man with an enlarged prostate and a mildly elevated PSA undergoes a nuclear medicine bone scan which shows significant uptake in the lungs. He has a normal calcium and phosphate. His CXR shows tiny diffuse calcific densities.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Alveolar microlithiasis

This condition falls under the 'common presentation of uncommon conditions' category. The patient develops tiny calculi in the alveoli during middle age. Typically the serum calcium and phosphate are normal and if the patient undergoes a nuclear medicine bone scan there is impressively high uptake diffusely in the lungs. Despite this the patient is often remarkably well.

Hyperparathyroidism

Parathyroid hormone acts to increase calcium levels either by promoting reabsorption in the kidneys or by acting on the osteoclasts of the bones and leads to increased bone resorption. This is seen as generalised osteopenia and cortical thinning, particularly of the subperiosteal bone.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually caused by an autonomous adenoma (alternatively parathyroid hyperplasia or a parathyroid carcinoma). Medullary nephrocalcinosis is most commonly caused by primary hyperparathyroidism but does also occur with secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a hyperplastic response of the parathyroid glands to the high phosphate and low calcium levels which accompany renal osteodystrophy. Soft tissue calcification is very much a feature of renal osteodystrophy. Confusingly the high circulating levels of phosphate in renal osteodystrophy leads to dystrophic mineralisation of trabecular bone which is seen as sclerosis; hence renal osteodystrophy is a cause of generalised increase in bone density despite hyperparathyroidism being a cause of osteopenia.

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs when a patient with secondary hyperparathyroidism (ie chronic overstimulation of the parathyroid glands) goes on to develop an autonomous adenoma.

Silicosis

Inhalation of silica leads to fibrosis. It is an occupational hazard associated with working in mines, quarries or with glass and ceramics. Chronic silicosis occurs following exposure over 10-20 years. Small nodules measuring a few millimeters in diameter form with an upper zone distribution (involvement of the upper zones is classical for inhalational diseases). Around 10% of these nodules calcify and this can be seen on imaging as multiple small foci of calcification in the upper zones. Lymph node enlargement is also a feature with eggshell calcification often quoted as a dominant feature of silicosis despite only being present in around 5% of patients. Intralobular septal thickening is often seen but pleural involvement is not a feature of silicosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man attends A+E with abdominal pain and is diagnosed with pancreatitis. He deteriorates rapidly, is intubated and ventilated and is admitted to the Intensive Care Unit. There his respiratory failure worsens although the capillary wedge pressure is normal. He undergoes a CT scan on day 2 of admission which is reported as showing Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following findings would be most likely to be seen?
options: Bilateral asymmetrical patchy opacification and pleural effusions
Bilateral symmetrical posterior dense consolidation and ground glass opacification
Perihilar ground glass opacification with pleural effusions
explanation:
ARDS is a severe life threatening entity that accelerates rapidly. Patients develop rapidly progressive dyspnoea, tachypnoea and hypoxia. As the alveoli fill with fluid and debris an arteriovenous (right-to-left) shunt develops since although the lungs may be well perfused, the under-aeration of the alveoli prevents gas exchange. Despite oxygenation therefore, the hypoxia becomes refractory to oxygen therapy as oxygenation can only improve a situation where the patient is ventilating adequately.

Causes of ARDS (Mnemonic - DICTIONARIES)

DIC

Infection

Caught drowning

Trauma

Inhalants (smoke, NO2)

Oxygen toxicity

Narcotics / drugs

Aspiration

Radiation

Includes pancreatitis

Emboli (fat, fluid)

Shock (septic, cardiogenic, anaphylactic, haemorrhagic)

The chest x-ray may be normal initially but descends into patchy opacification and which becomes confluent and extensive within hours, involving most if not all of both hemithoraces. On a CT scan there is usually extensive ground glass opacification and dependant consolidation. The presence of non-dependant consolidation should raise the possibility of superadded infection at any stage of the course of the disease.

Image 2: Confluent opacification

The changes within a lung can be charted according to a timeline:

Time

Lung pathology

Radiological findings

First 12 hours

Microemboli of fibrin and platelets

During this time there may be no radiological findings

12-24 hours

Interstitial oedema

Air space opacities

Dependant consolidation

24-48 hours

Interstitial and alveolar oedema, microatelectasis

Air space opacities

Dependant consolidation

5-7 days

Hyaline membrane formation, hyperplasia of type 2 pneumocytes

Reticular opacities and decreasing consolidation

7-14 days

Collagen deposition and fibrosis, often with superadded infection

Non dependant consolidation (suggesting infection)

Subpleural reticulation and honeycombing (sequelae of developing fibrosis)

If patients do survive they are initially often left with fibrotic changes in the lungs but many patients actually experience surprisingly few long-term sequelae. The lungs gradually remodel and resolve the fibrotic changes that take place in the intermediate term.

The wedge capillary pressure is measured via a Swan-Ganz catheter inserted peripherally and fed through the right side of the heart to reach a branch of the (usually left) pulmonary artery. A small balloon can be inflated to temporarily occlude this artery and a tiny transducer at the tip of the catheter measures the pressure as the balloon deflates (the mechanism is similar to blood pressure recording via an upper arm cuff).

Wedge capillary pressure is a surrogate measure for left atrial pressures which rise with left ventricular failure or problems with the aortic and mitral valves. If the capillary wedge pressure is elevated then a cardiac cause should be strongly suspected. Non-cardiogenic causes of ARDS should not elevate the capillary wedge pressure.

The silhouette (pronounced as: sil-o-wet) sign has a leading role in the interpretation of chest xrays. It occurs when two structures are adjacent to one another and it is therefore not possible to see where one begins and the other ends on a CXR. In order to see all the way around any structure it must have a difference in density between it and any structure touching it; this is called ‘contrast’. The silhouette sign is useful because it can be used to define the anatomical location of pathology.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a 10 pack year history of smoking undergoes a CT scan of her chest.
prompt: Which feature would make LAM more likely than Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis?
explanation:
Although LCH classically occurs in young smokers, there is no reason that LAM cannot occur in smokers. The two share a prevalent age range and have some overlapping features. However, although effusions can rarely be seen in LCH, the presence of a chylous effusion is highly suggestive of LAM. Some of the other pertinent features are detailed below.

LCH

LAM

Cysts

Spontaneous pneumothorax

Effusions (Rare with LCH, much more likely with LAM - would be chylous)

Young patient

Smoker

Female

Hilar lymph nodes (rarely)

Mediastinal lymph nodes

Honeycombing

Increased lung volume

Spares costophrenic angles

1/3rd have renal AMLs

Histiocytosis (also known as Langerhans cell histiocytosis - LCH)

There are three separate forms of this disease:

Eosinophilic granuloma (70%) – a limited version confined to the skeleton in children or young adults. Clinically presents as fever, raised WCC and ESR with painful bony lesions. In the skull these have a typical ‘beveled edge’ or ‘hole within a hole’ appearance or can be seen as a ‘button sequestrum’. In the spine it is one of the main causes of vertebra plana.

Hand-Schüller-Christian Disease (20%) – classically a triad of destructive bony lesions, diabetes insipidus and exophthalmos. In a quarter of these patients the lungs are involved with cyst formation and spontaneous pneumothoraces possible. Nodule formation, fibrosis and honeycombing is also seen.

Letterer-Siwe Disease (10%) – a fulminant multi-organ variant affecting very young infants

There is a strong association with smoking for patients who develop pulmonary features of LCH. Heavy smoking causes an accumulation of Langerhans cells and hence, as with other inspiration-related lung diseases, there is a predilection for the upper zones. The Langerhans cells can collect with other cells and become small granulomas seen as small lung nodules. Despite being a type of fibrotic lung disease the lung volumes can be increased. Small lung cysts form and there is a risk of spontaneous pneumothorax. There is usually sparing of the costophrenic angles which can be a key finding.

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)

LAM can go misdiagnosed for many years as emphysema. It occurs almost exclusively in women of childbearing age (usually non-smokers), and quite often a history of spontaneous pneumothorax is given. Radiologically there are numerous small cystic spaces surrounded by normal lung. A chylous pleural effusion (negative Hounsfield units) is reasonably specific. The main differential diagnosis would be histiocytosis which tends to be associated with smoking, classically spares the costophrenic angles and gives small nodules but both can present with spontaneous pneumothorax and give small cysts. The lung volumes in LAM will remain normal, or can be slightly increased. The same is also true for histiocytisis which is counter-intuitive (and thus more noteworthy) given it is a fibrotic lung disease.

stem: A 56-year-old man complaining of chest pain undergoes a CT chest that shows a cardiac carcinoid disease.
prompt: What are the most likely features that will be seen?
options: Prolapse of a soft tissue density mass through the mitral valve
explanation:
The spectrum of cardiac carcinoid disease encompasses the physical plaque deposits of metastatic disease as well as the valve damage caused by secretion of vasoactive substances from the tumour load. Classically the right side of the heart is most affected because most of the primary lesions, as well as hepatic metastases, secrete into the right-sided circulation. In around a quarter of cases the primary carcinoid tumour is located in the lungs and so in these patients the left sided heart valves will be affected moreso/if at all than the right.

Prolapse of a soft tissue density mass through the mitral valve is a classic description for a myxoma however this feature is seen on Ultrasound predominantly, as well as potentially on cardiac MRI.

A low attenuation mass without calcification is probably describing a lipoma.

stem: The coronary arteries
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the coronary arteries is true?
options: The left coronary artery arises from the aorta below the left cusp of the aortic valve
The left coronary artery supplies the right atrium
The right coronary artery is larger than the left
The right coronary artery supplies the SA and AV nodes
The right coronary artery supplies the entire interventricular septum
explanation:
The left coronary artery arises from the aorta above the left cusp of the aortic valve. It supplies the left atrium, left ventricle, intraventricular septum and part of the left branch bundle of His. It is larger than the right coronary artery.

It passes between the left side of the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle and then bifurcates into the left anterior descending artery (LAD), which is also called the anterior interventricular branch, and the left circumflex artery (LCA). Sometimes an additional artery arises at the bifurcation called the ramus or intermediate artery.

The LAD follows the anterior interventricular groove towards the apex of the heart and then continues to the posterior surface of the heart to anastamose with the posterior interventricular branch.

The LCA follows the anterior atrioventricular groove to the left border of the heart and then proceeds to the posterior surface. It then gives rise to the left marginal branch, which follows the left border of the heart.

The right coronary artery arises above the right cusp of the aortic valve. It supplies the right atrium, the SA and AV nodes and the posterior part of the interventricular septum.

It runs along the right atrioventricular groove before branching. The right marginal artery arises first and then the right coronary artery continues on to the posterior surface of the heart, still running in the right atrioventricular groove. The posterior descending artery (PDA), which is also called the posterior interventricular artery, arises next and then follows the posterior interventricular groove towards the apex of the heart.

stem: You are reviewing the imaging of a 50-year-old man who was seen in the respiratory clinic with ongoing shortness of breath. His chest radiograph shows abnormalities in both bases and he went on to have an HRCT. This shows dense honeycombing to both bases and costophrenic angles.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) also known as either Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) or cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis (CFA)

This is classically a disease of previously fit middle-aged men with a reasonably long (>6 month) history of shortness of breath and cough. Volume loss is prevalent and there is a classical apico-basilar gradient meaning that the lower zones are much more affected than the upper zones. Honeycombing is classical, particularly subpleural honeycombing. When secondary to a condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or a drug it is known as usual interstitial pneumonia. Overall the prognosis for this condition is extremely poor; worse than that for many common cancers.

There is much overlap in the features of the various different fibrotic lung diseases.

Therefore, look for specific features which are most strongly associated with the different conditions. The table below (despite appearances) simplifies the overall situation significantly and is inadequate for real life radiology but does provide a framework on which to build further understanding of these conditions.

Diagnosis

Features

IPF = UIP = CFA

Macrocystic honeycombing, apicobasilar gradient

NSIP

stem: A cardiology patient needs a diagnostic coronary angiogram but is known to have a chronically occluded left common iliac artery.
prompt: What is the best approach?
explanation:
The femoral approach has for a long time been the traditional approach for a coronary angiogram owing to its relative ease. The vessel is large, easily accessible and leads on a reasonably straight course to the heart. By comparison the radial and ulnar arteries are smaller, at greater risk of spasm and can undergo greater tortuosity thereby necessitating greater operator skill. However the radial approach is gaining significant ground as an alternative to the femoral approach and in many centres worldwide is now the preferred approach. Despite the difficulty of the procedure, a radial approach boasts better morbidity and mortality statistics and is associated with faster recovery times than femoral access. Additionally, severe aortoiliac disease is seen as a relative contraindication to femoral puncture.

Prior to a radial approach the patient should be tested with Allens test to ensure patency of both radial and ulnar arteries. The ulnar artery is smaller and less easily accessible than the radial artery although some studies have been performed to evaluate its suitability for access.

CT angiography is also gaining ground as an alternative to any invasive diagnostic angiography. The advantages of a non-invasive technique in the outpatient setting are clear however the current level of availability is insufficient to provide a diagnostic service for the primary management of myocardial infarction.

The azygo-oesophageal recess is formed by the interface of the right lung and the mediastinal reflection of the azygos vein.

stem: A 65-year-old man being staged for his lung cancer arrives for an FDG exam.
prompt: For which of the following reasons should the scan be delayed or re-scheduled?
options: He had a black coffee the previous afternoon
He has fasted for less than 8 hours
He went to the gym the previous afternoon
explanation:
FDG imaging relies on glucose uptake being increased in tissues of interest which are more metabolically active than non-target tissues. Hence the patient must be fasted such that the FDG given is taken up rapidly enough to produce an image.

FDG is renally excreted. Patients with a poor renal function are at risk of enduring a higher dose than those with a normal renal function. However assuming the dose is correctly adjusted down there is no reason such patients cannot undergo PET/CT scanning.

Insulin treatment does not preclude imaging, and indeed helps reduce the extracellular glucose concentration thereby improving the quality of scans acquired later. There should be at least a 4 hour gap between the last insulin dose and the FDG tracer dose time.

The literature on fasting varies and different organizations have suggested slightly different fasting windows. The most conservative of these is 6 hours.

Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine must be avoided for at least 12 hours prior to the scan.

Exercise should be avoided for 24, if not 48 hours prior to the scan.

stem: A 36-year-old woman has a cardiac MRI for investigation of shortness of breath. There was straightening of the interventricular septum, among other findings.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Inflammation of the pericardium is termed pericarditis and leads to fibrous thickening. Most commonly this occurs either post-operatively in patients undergoing cardiac surgery or as an idiopathic entity although historically it was tuberculosis which was the most common cause of pericarditis. The diagnosis is predominantly clinical with symptoms such as malaise or dyspnoea and signs such as neck vein distension or paradoxical movement of the JVP. On cross sectional imaging thickening of the pericardium to greater than 2mm can be seen and the fibrosis causes a restriction in distensibility. The right ventricle, being more compliant than the left, becomes flattened and furthermore there can be curvature of the septum towards the left. Elsewhere, if the field of view permits, accessory signs such as pleural effusions and even ascites may be seen.

Pulmonary Emboli

There is some cross-over of the signs and symptoms of pericarditis and a large lobar embolus. On CT, if the embolus is large enough to cause right ventricular strain the septum can sometimes appear bowed with reflux of IV contrast into the hepatic veins.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of sarcoidosis?
prompt: Select only one answer.
explanation:
Sarcoidosis is known as the great mimic as it can appear in almost any way it chooses. Classical thoracic sarcoidosis is seen as perilymphatic nodules and interlobular septal thickening in association with mediastinal and hilar lymph node enlargement. Eggshell calcification is a feature often associated with sarcoidosis and does become increasingly common with disease duration but still only affects a fifth of patients.

Among features not typical of sarcoidosis, pleural disease (including pleural effusion) is important to note and should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses where present. Similarly cavitation of lymph nodes is also atypical.

stem: A 64-year-old man undergoes a left pneumonectomy for lung cancer. He recovers well post-operatively and is reviewed in clinic shortly after discharge at two weeks post operation.
prompt: Which of the following CXR appearances, if not seen pre-operatively, would not be expected at this time?
options: An air fluid level in the left hemithorax at approximately two thirds of the way up the chest
Complete opacification of the left hemithorax
explanation:
Overall post-pneumonectomy changes are features of volume loss with fluid accumulation in the affected hemithorax.

As the now empty hemithorax gradually fills with fluid an air-fluid level is to be expected. This should reach approximately half-way up the chest on a CXR by day 4 or day 5 and should reach at least 66%, if not 100%, of the height of the chest on a CXR after a fortnight. Ipsilateral mediastinal shift also usually takes place owing to the volume loss although this is not an absolute finding; Some patients will have no mediastinal shift. Diaphragmatic elevation would be an expected finding, diaphragmatic flattening would not.

Post-operative complications of a pneumonectomy include:

5-10% bronchopulmonary fistula

Contralateral tracheal shift

Reduction in height of the fluid level on sequential films

5% ARDS

5% Pulmonary oedema

<5% empyema

Post-pneumonectomy syndrome

This occurs when hyperexpansion of the remaining lung displaces the heart, with rotation of the heart in an anticlockwise fashion along its long axis.

This develops in the first year and usually affects young adults or children. Patients develop exertional dyspnoea or recurrent infections

stem: You are reviewing a trauma CT scan for a 36-year-old patient following a multi-vehicle accident. There is an obvious pelvic fracture with active haemorrhage from an internal iliac artery branch.
prompt: How should this best be managed? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Arterial bleeding from pelvic fractures

Pelvic fractures in the context of trauma are a cause of significant morbidity and mortality. Life threatening haemorrhage may be caused by arterial bleeding or other sources such as the fractured bones themselves, and the pelvic venous structures. External fixation is one of the few means of managing acute haemorrhage in the pre-hospital setting however for arterial bleeding it is far less effective at tamponading ongoing haemorrhage. It remains the treatment of choice for bone bleeding or venous bleeding.

Catheter angiography and embolisation is the most effective method to control arterial haemorrhage. If the patient is haemodynamically unstable due to an arterial pelvic haemorrhage, catheter embolisation still provides the best hope for managing the patient successfully. Even if the patient has abdominal injuries which are likely to necessitate open abdominal trauma surgery, studies have shown that arterial pelvic bleeding should still be controlled via catheter embolisation prior to their open surgery.
